#3472. Eight Important Router Settings You Should Check (or Change)

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Your router is a key piece of your home network, as it connects all of your other devices to the internet. This also makes it a highly valuable target for attackers and can leave your data vulnerable—especially if you simply plug your router in with its default settings unchanged. Whether your router is brand new or it's been a while since you audited your existing setup, these are the key settings to check and change right now.

Your router's security protocol determines how encryption and authentication work to protect data that's transmitted over your network. WPA3 Personal is the newest standard and the most secure, so if it's available on your router, enable it. It's compatible with devices that support Wi-Fi 6. Some older devices may not work with WPA3, in which case the WPA2/WPA3 Transitional mixed mode is a good alternative. At minimum, set your router to WPA2 Personal (AES).

Some routers ship with factory default login credentials, which are the username and password you need to access your device's admin dashboard. (This is not the same as your network name or wifi password, which you set up later.) Default router passwords are searchable online, which leaves your router's admin settings open to anyone. Once you get into your dashboard for the first time, change the default credentials and enable two-factor authentication for your admin account if available.

While some newer routers do have unique, device-specific defaults, it's a good idea to check this setting and ensure it's secure. If you're prompted to create custom admin credentials during the setup process, do it.

Your network name, or SSID, is how your network appears when you search for available wifi. By default, this may be the name of the router brand or a short string of characters, but you should choose something unique to your network. Make sure there's no identifying personal information, such as your name or house number. While you may be tempted to hide your network and obscure your SSID, this may actually make your information less secure, so keep this setting disabled. You can, however, add "_nomap" to the end of your network name, which prevents your router's physical coordinates from being mapped by location databases.

The password to access your network should also be unique and secure and should not include obvious personal information. One option to keep it memorable and easy to type is to create a passphrase using five to seven unrelated words that, combined, have at least 16 characters.

Being able to log into your router's admin dashboard from anywhere may be useful if you have complex networking needs or troubleshooting issues that often have to be addressed when you're away from home, but it also leaves an entry point open for attackers. Turn off remote management to prevent anyone from accessing your dashboard unless they are on your network. (This is also a great reason to have strong, unique admin credentials.)

Two additional settings that leave your network vulnerable are Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) and Universal Plug and Play (UPnP). The former lets users connect to your network with a PIN, which can be vulnerable to brute-force attacks. The latter allows smart devices to easily connect to your network—but this also allows malware to spread more readily. You may need to have UPnP on in order to connect devices initially but should disable it afterward.

Any easy win for your network security is segmenting traffic to different networks, so if one is compromised, the data on the others remain unaffected. Many wifi routers have a "guest mode," which creates a separate SSID and password that you can share with visitors instead of giving them your primary network credentials. You can also set up a separate network for all of your smart home and IoT devices so exploitable vulnerabilities in these devices don't put your computers, phones, and other connected devices at risk too.

Routers run a type of software—called firmware—just like any other device. Firmware controls the router's core functions and is not immune to vulnerabilities, which can be exploited by bad actors. And, just like other types of software, manufacturers occasionally push updates to patch these flaws. Check your router's dashboard to see if automatic updates are toggled on. Some devices require an opt-in for auto updates during setup, so you should enable them if they are off. Some routers may even require manual updates—in this case, set a monthly or quarterly (at minimum) calendar reminder to check for patches.

#3471. Spider-Man’s Dark Reboot Universe Unveils Twisted New Design For Classic Villain

Warning! This post contains SPOILERS for Midnight Spider-Man #2

Marvel's new Midnight Universe has begun, featuring dark and horrific new takes on classic heroes in an alt universe unlike anything we've seen before. However, the latest issue of Midnight Spider-Man has confirmed that villains are receiving just as terrifying redesigns as well.

As seen in the first issue of Midnight Spider-Man, this dark new continuity's Peter Parker has become a truly grotesque David Cronenberg-style body-horror version of a human-spider hybrid, the result of twisted Oscorp experiments in the pursuit of eternal life. Contrasting with the classic Spider-Man motto, "With great power comes great responsibility", the darker world and circumstances surrounding Peter have instead instilled the phrase: "power makes monsters." Now that Peter has become a monster himself, his future looks to be all kinds of horrifying.

Now, Midnight Spider-Man #2 by Phillip Kennedy Johnson and Scietronc has debuted a brand-new version of Doctor Octopus, one that's easily more disturbing than any version seen before in the pages of Marvel Comics.

The story in Midnight Spider-Man #2 is aptly titled "The Eight-Handed Man," giving readers our first look at Otto Octavius and his role as a lead researcher at Oscorp behind the Augustine Project and the company's mission to achieve eternal life via twisted experiments involving animal-human hybrids. Initially shown as a reclusive germaphobe who hates interacting with foreign contaminants and individuals outside his lab, an incredibly diminutive Otto keeps himself isolated behind glass with various metal pins sticking out of his head.

The lab itself is full of dissection tables with various genetically mutated specimens that have gruesomely been ripped apart by his "assistants". Rather than having his traditional four robotic arms, this dark new version of Doctor Octopus controls four human beings through cybernetic brain implants somewhat resembling the classic tentacles. All of their individual humanity looks to have been stripped away, leaving them as nothing more than remote-controlled extensions of Octavius. Likewise, Octavius even threatens to turn Felicia Hardy into his next assistant should she fail to recover the spider that escaped in the new series' first issue.

Having wound up in Peter's backpack, the large radioactive spider ultimately fused with Peter and embedded itself in his chest. Currently unaware of this monstrous transformation, Otto desperately wants the spider back, and for Felicia to ensure that Peter signs a contract of employment to start working at Oscorp itself.

Ultimately, this super dark intro for Midnight Doc Ock makes it clear that as monstrous as Peter Parker might have just become in this dark new universe, Oscorp is the true and much bigger monster behind it all.

Nevertheless, it's extremely unsettling to see "Spider-Man" launching himself at Felicia Hardy (perhaps a future Midnight Black Cat?) and her men when they come to Peter's house, ripping the security guards to shreds with all kinds of blood and gore, leaving the house with only Felicia alive and paralyzed with fear. Clearly, this is going to be one of the scariest and most violent Spider-Man ever seen.

With the first issue strongly implying that the spider killed Uncle Ben before fusing with Peter, the grief and horror that will come once Peter discovers this will likely be what fully turns him against Oscorp (he had been more optimistic about joining them and turning them into a force for good from within, despite Uncle Ben suing them for their involvement in the deaths of Peter's parents).

Assuming Peter will find a way to control or at least direct his monstrous impulses toward those responsible, it follows that Midnight Spider-Man will likely wage a one-man war against Oscorp in future issues. As such, his new status as a human-spider hybrid will no doubt be seen as a major breakthrough by Octavius, making a confrontation between the two more than inevitable in the issues to come.

Midnight Spider-Man #2 is on sale now from Marvel Comics.

#3470. 8 Books Like Harry Potter, but Better

It is an undeniable fact that the Harry Potter novels are among the most influential book series of all time. With over 600 million copies sold worldwide, J.K. Rowling’s fantasy novels have made an indelible mark on the genre, shaping both literature and global culture. That said, just because it’s the best-selling book series of all time doesn’t mean it’s the best book series of all time.

There have been several great fantasy books released over the decades that share similarities with Harry Potter but deliver much better stories and experiences. Not all of them have achieved comparable levels of fame and success, but their quality and significance to the genre are undeniable. With that in mind, here’s our selection of books that are like Harry Potter, but better.

Ursula K. Le Guin’s A Wizard of Earthsea is a classic fantasy novel that’s widely credited with establishing the magical academy setting later used in the Harry Potter series. Set in the titular archipelago, the book follows Ged, a young and impulsive mage who accidentally unleashes a shadow into the world. Haunted by this shadow, Ged sets off on a journey, mastering his powers and gaining deeper wisdom to confront it.

A Wizard of Earthsea may have a few cosmetic similarities to Harry Potter, but the novel exists on a whole other level, taking a philosophical approach to magic that’s about a lot more than magic duels and good vs. evil. A pioneering work of modern fantasy, the book won the 1969 Boston Globe-Horn Book Award and was one of the final recipients of the Lewis Carroll Shelf Award in 1979. It’s had a strong influence on the fantasy genre ever since and was followed by five more books that collectively make up the Earthsea Cycle.

The debut novel of Irish playwright Derek Landy, Skulduggery Pleasant (also known as Skulduggery Pleasant: Scepter of the Ancients or simply The Scepter of the Ancients), is the first book of the novel series. A genre-bending urban fantasy mystery, the book introduces the young Stephanie Edgley, who inherits her late uncle’s estate and soon finds herself targeted by the forces of a dangerous necromancer. Thankfully, she gets some magical help from the titular mage, a skeleton detective/wizard.

Skulduggery Pleasant was quite favorably received at the time of its publication and went on to win the Red House Children's Book Award and the Hampshire Book Award, as well as several other accolades. It’s an engaging dark fantasy that easily rivals Harry Potter for entertainment, blending horror, mystery, and fantasy, with a relatable protagonist and a fascinating cast of interesting characters. The novel has since spawned a massive series that includes 27 books, the latest, A Small Matter of Impending Catastrophe, released in 2025.

One of the books most commonly recommended to fans of Harry Potter, Percy Jackson & the Olympians: The Lightning Thief is the first novel in Rick Riordan’s bestselling Camp Half-Blood Chronicles franchise. The book introduces readers to 12-year-old Percy Jackson, the demigod son of the Greek god Poseidon, who discovers the secret of his parentage just in time to be caught in the middle of a potential war. His only option to prevent this catastrophe is to head out on a cross-country quest alongside his friends, Annabeth Chase and Grover Underwood.

Witty, energetic, and highly endearing, The Lightning Thief is a fun take on Greek mythology that takes audiences into the fascinating world of ancient gods and monsters. It’s an engaging coming-of-age fantasy novel and a great entry point into the Camp Half-Blood Chronicles, which has since evolved into a massive world. The novel was adapted as a 2010 film by Chris Columbus and more recently adapted for the Disney+ series Percy Jackson and the Olympians, co-created by Riordan.

The first novel of Eoin Colfer’s book series, Artemis Fowl is a young adult fantasy novel centered on the titular character, a 12-year-old criminal mastermind. With the assistance of his loyal bodyguard Butler, Artemis sets out to capture an elf police officer, setting off a major hostage crisis in the fairy world. The book was followed by ten sequels split across two cycles.

Since its publication in 2001, Artemis Fowl has been highly acclaimed by critics and very popular with readers, developing a sizable fanbase. Combining a sharp sense of humor with intelligent plotting, the book and the series it spawned are easily among the best of 21st-century fantasy, with the series selling more than 21 million copies around the world. A film based on the novel was released in 2020 to highly negative reviews, but though that adaptation was a failure, an animated series is currently in development.

First published in Germany in 2003, Inkheart is a young adult fantasy novel by Cornelia Funke that’s the first book in the series. The novel follows Meggie, a young girl who lives with her father Mortimer, a bookbinder. A visit by a strange man named Dustfinger upends Meggie's and Mortimer’s lives, and Meggie learns that her father has a rare ability to conjure things out of books by reading aloud from them.

A fascinating fantasy book that’s partly a coming-of-age story and partly a celebration of storytelling, Inkheart was quite favorably received at the time of its publication. The novel became a finalist for the 2004 BookSense Book of the Year Award for Children's Literature and won other accolades as well. The book was followed by three sequels, 2005’s Inkspell, 2007’s Inkdeath, and 2023’s The Colour of Revenge, and a film adaptation was released in 2008.

A cozy fantasy romance novel written by Sangu Mandanna, The Very Secret Society of Irregular Witches centers on young witch Mika Moon. The story is set in a world where witches live in secrecy and isolation. Born (and orphaned) in India but now living in the UK, Mika deals with her loneliness by making fake roleplay videos where she “pretends” to be a witch, but when someone recognizes her magic as real, Mika finds herself caring for three young witches living with non-magical adults in a place called Nowhere House.

Sangu Mandanna's earlier books before The Very Secret Society of Irregular Witches were all middle-grade and young adult fiction, and the novel is her adult debut. As such, the book is suited to a more mature audience than the average Harry Potter reader, but it is a great read for adults who grew up dreaming of Hogwarts. There’s no magical school, and the conflicts of the book are more interpersonal than world-ending, but it’s a delightful read that’s as cozy and warm as a Studio Ghibli movie.

Lev Grossman’s The Magicians is the first book of the new adult fantasy trilogy of the same name. The novel is centered on Quentin Coldwater, a young high school graduate who grew up reading a Chronicles of Narnia-esque book series set in a magical world called Fillory. After he is accepted into a secret magical college, Quentin discovers that Fillory and its magic are real — and a lot more dangerous than he thought.

Often compared to Harry Potter, The Magicians’ first and most obvious distinction is that its magical school is a university, where magical studies involve a lot less wand-waving and a lot more actual studying. Beyond that, the book and its sequels explore significantly more complex and delightfully weird concepts that are highly engaging for fans of modern fantasy. A TV adaptation premiered on Syfy in 2015, and The Magicians was followed by two sequels, 2011’s The Magician King and 2014’s The Magician’s Land, as well as two comic book series.

Written by Philip Pullman, His Dark Materials is a dark fantasy trilogy that consists of 1995’s Northern Lights (published as The Golden Compass in North America), 1997’s The Subtle Knife, and 2000’s The Amber Spyglass. The first book introduces the central character, Lyra Belacqua, a young child from a universe where people’s souls manifest outside their bodies as animal companions. Lyra’s adventures bring her into conflict with the theocratic rulers of her world, the Magisterium, as she learns more about the nature of the mysterious multiversal substance known as Dust.

Combining parallel universes and dark matter with fantasy concepts and a compelling coming-of-age story, His Dark Materials is a class apart from other fantasy books. A true fantasy masterpiece, the trilogy has earned critical acclaim and won several accolades, including the Carnegie Medal. The books have inspired multiple adaptations, including a 2007 film and a BBC-HBO TV series, and the original trilogy was followed by four short works and a sequel trilogy, the latest of which is 2025’s The Rose Field.

His dark materials was particularly bad in my opinion, I did not enjoy the story at all. Inkheart was good, but not complex. Of these, I have read inkheart, Percy jackson, and his dark materials, and I can say that in my opinion, none of them is better than Harry Potter. #3469. The iPhone Duo Is Getting Face Unlock

Apple dropped iOS 27.2.1 last week, patching a handful of security vulnerabilities and bugs—including two iMessage flaws that let people read messages they shouldn't. But while most of us are running this version (or should install it as soon as possible), others are running something different—iOS 27.3.

Apple is currently beta testing the third major update in the iOS 27 era, and anyone—developer and public tester alike—is free to install it at their leisure. With it, comes the return of the Health app, vertical Safari tabs, and Siri AI app actions, among other new features. But for users of Apple's first foldable, the iPhone Duo, iOS 27.3 brings two rather notable changes—both of which are for the better.

With the second iOS 27.3 developer beta, Apple is introducing face unlock for the iPhone Duo. The foldable famously ships with Touch ID, the first new iPhone since the third-gen iPhone SE to do so. While that isn't a problem per se, many of us are used to unlocking our iPhones with our faces. This update just lets new Duo owners keep up with that muscle memory.

Now, take note: This isn't Face ID. No software update can introduce new hardware, so the iPhone Duo still doesn't have the camera tech required to power Apple's Face ID system. As such, the Duo's face unlock is likely not as secure as Face ID on other iPhones. Perhaps that's why your iPhone Duo will require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. This feature seems to be one of pure convenience: If you want to be able to unlock your Duo with your face (at least, some of the time), you can.

What's more, this isn't a default setting. If you're running the beta, or if you're reading this after iOS 27.3 drops, you can find the option in Settings > Touch ID & Passcode.

Apple made a big deal about the continuity involved with opening and closing the iPhone Duo. As you do, your content moves with you seamlessly—a very Apple thing to do. That said, you might expect folding the Duo to lock it, but it doesn't. You need to hit the side button to actually put the phone to sleep.

iOS 27.3 changes that. If you so choose, you can enable a setting to lock your Duo whenever you close it. That won't work for everyone, of course—some users may still want to move between modes without worrying about locking their Duos. But for those who would rather lock their devices whenever they fold them up, the new option is under Settings > Display & Brightness.

The Oura Ring 5 holds the title of the "world's smallest smart ring", with a focus on a slim design and lightweight barely-there feel.

After wearing the Oura Ring 5 for five months, I must say that it lives up to its title. Not once have I ever felt any discomfort from wearing the ring, with its sleep design never interfering with my sleep. Thanks to the sizing kit, it fits like a glove, too.

The Oura Ring 5's fit was a breath of fresh air compared to the Apple Watch Ultra that I wore to bed for a few months before I obtained the Oura Ring 5. Granted, the Apple Watch Ultra is a lot bigger and bulkier than the newer Apple Watch models, such as the Apple Watch 12.

But all Apple Watches are exactly that: watches. I find any wristwatch uncomfortable to wear in bed, particularly smartwatches with heavy screens and tight straps (you need plenty of skin contact for tracking accuracy). But that's a personal preference and if you don't mind something bulky on your wrist in bed, you might sleep happily in the Apple Watch 12.

As for the Garmin, the lead tester in our Garmin Index Sleep Monitor review found the armband design to be surprisingly comfortable and lightweight. The band is available in two sizes (S-M and L-XL), and its screen-free design means it isn't weighed down by heavy monitors.

When it comes down to it, the Oura, Apple, and Garmin sleep trackers share a lot of core sleep tracking features. For example, not only do all three tell you how long you slept, but also how much of that sleep duration was spent in deep sleep, REM sleep, and core sleep (along with how long your night-time awakenings last). They also all provide sleep scores, which measure your overall sleep quality on a scale of 1 to 100.

You can find the key sleep metrics in the Oura app, Garmin Connect app, and the Apple Health app respectively. For the screenless Oura and Garmin, this is the only way to view your sleep data. But you get immediate feedback from your Apple Watch via the Vitals app on the monitor.

The Oura Ring 5 is designed to provide more sleep tracking accuracy than the Oura Ring 4, with a build that improves the sensors' contact with skin and 12% more accuracy in its overnight Heart Rate Variability (HRV) monitoring.

I've found the Oura Ring one of the most dependable consumer sleep trackers on the market. It's especially good at knowing when you're asleep vs awake; studies show up to 96% accuracy when compared to clinical polysomnography (PSG).

I can see the Oura Ring 5's accuracy first hand. When I wore the Oura Ring 5 and the Apple Watch (Ultra) at the same time, I felt the Oura Ring's data reflected how I felt in the morning more accurately than the Apple Watch. For instance, my Apple Watch sleep scores are always much higher than my Oura Ring — despite regularly getting under seven hours of sleep.

That said, the Apple Watch does provide a sleep apnea detection tool (available on the Apple Watch Series 10 and up), which analyzes your breathing patterns to detect disturbances that might signal sleep apnea.

Meanwhile, the Garmin Index Sleep Monitor provides a readiness score, which tells you how prepared your body is to handle daily activities (such as workouts) based on your sleep data.

Our lead tester for the Garmin Index Sleep Monitor, Eve Davies, said that the Garmin is "more focused on overnight breathing rates, oxygen levels and respiration rates — is essentially more ‘nerdy’ and geared towards athletic recovery". For data lovers, there's a lot to unpack.

It's also worth mentioning that the Oura Ring 5's sleep latency metric is missing from the Apple Watch and Index Sleep Monitor. And its unique circadian scoring, which uses sleep data over time to identify your sleep chronotype, can help you identify how well your sleep routine aligns with your circadian rhythm.

The Oura Ring 5 is designed to provide around six to nine days of battery life on a single charge. A full charge (from zero to 100) is said to take up to 80 minutes, though I find it charges much faster than this.

That said, I've never found that my ring's battery life has lasted nine days (or even a full week), but this may be due to the fact that I wear a size 7 — the smaller sizes have a shorter battery life.

However, the lifespan of an Oura Ring is that of a giant tortoise when compared with the Apple Watch. The Apple Watch requires daily charging, with the latest 12th Generation's battery life lasting no longer than 24 hours.

The Garmin has quite a lengthy battery life, lasting up to eight nights (however, this can depend on your sleep duration). However, you also wear it less than the Oura Ring 5 or Apple Watch — if you strapped it to yourself all day, expect that battery life to go right down.

✅ You want in-depth sleep tracking: The Oura Ring 5's accuracy is renowned, while its unique sleep features (such as its Body Clock feature) sets it apart.

✅ You value optimal sleep comfort: Thanks to a custom fit and a sleek, lightweight build, the Oura Ring 5 is perfect for a barely-there feel.

✅ You don't own an iPhone: You need an iPhone to set up your Apple Watch, so consider the Oura Ring 5 if you're an Android user.

✅ You don't want to pay monthly fees: The Apple Watch has no hidden subscription costs.

✅ You want immediate feedback: With a screen to view your metrics, the Apple Watch is the only option that doesn't require fiddling about with an app.

✅ You want more versatility: There's a lot more to the Apple Watch than sleep tracking, including highly-rated fitness tracking, and there are plenty of models to suit your requirements.

✅ You want the most budget-friendly tracker: The Garmin Index Sleep Monitor is never sold over $170, and you can reliably find it on sale during holiday seasons.

✅ You just want a sleep tracker: While the Oura Ring 5 and Apple Watch put a lot of energy into fitness and health tracking, the Garmin Index Sleep Monitor is strictly for sleep tracking.

✅ You want a long battery life: The Garmin Index Sleep Monitor can last up to eight nights on a single charge.

#3466. Apple TV’s New 10-Part Sci-Fi Series Replaces Prime Video’s Canceled William Gibson Show

William Gibson is one of the most influential authors in the sci-fi genre. Often credited for pioneering the cyberpunk subgenre, his most seminal novel, Neuromancer, remains a sci-fi masterpiece in 2026. Despite the timelessness and popularity of his literary work, however, his cyberpunk stories and books have hardly been adapted for the screen.

While many video games, movies, and TV shows have loosely drawn from his work, there are only a handful of direct mainstream adaptations of his stories. Two of these, Johnny Mnemonic and New Rose Hotel, premiered in the '90s and struggled to leave their mark. One, titled The Peripheral, premiered on Prime Video in 2022 before being canceled after one season.

Considering the long-standing legacy and influence of William Gibson's work, it is unfortunate that none of his adaptations have worked too well on the screen so far. However, this will soon likely change. Apple TV is now adapting one of William Gibson's most iconic cyberpunk sci-fi books, Neuromancer, which has the potential to become one of the biggest events of the genre in this decade.

Most cyberpunk TV shows and movies focus a little too much on the visual aspect, featuring neon-soaked cityscapes and edgy characters. Prime Video's The Peripheral, on the other hand, truly understood the essence of William Gibson's near-future cyberpunk. In its 2032 timeline, the show features a very familiar, economically broken rural America.

Technology is deeply grafted onto the blue-collar lives of regular people. There are 3-D printed pharmaceuticals, while even veterans with disabilities use military implants called "haptics." The series also reveals its central VR technology as a form of escapism for the main characters who place it in a run-down trailer.

Then comes the show's 2099 timeline where it contrasts 2032's "low lives" with London's high-tech and elite. This is when The Peripheral also introduces "The Jackpot," to reveal the high stakes of its apocalyptic conflict and how humanity's unchecked ambition in the future has pushed civilization to the brink of collapse.

In its 8-episode runtime, Prime Video's The Peripheral did enough to earn more follow-ups and expand its sci-fi vision in season 2. It was a rare adaptation that embraced the hard-edged sci-fi and weirdness of its source material. Unfortunately, despite being promising, its renewal was reversed by Prime Video after SAG-AFTRA and Writers Guild of America's strikes in 2023.

The works of many sci-fi authors, like Philip K. Dick, are not easy to adapt. Yet, Philip K. Dick's stories have already received multiple worthy on-screen adaptations. William Gibson's adaptations, in contrast, have almost been cursed. The ones like Johnny Mnemonic became cult classics, but never achieved mainstream acclaim or success.

Meanwhile, The Peripheral had immense potential, but failed to last beyond one season. After being considered "unfilmable" for quite some time, William Gibson's Neuromancer is finally being adapted by Apple TV. And so far, it looks like the show will finally spell redemption for William Gibson's adaptations.

Apple TV's history of bringing challenging adaptations like Isaac Asimov's Foundation to the screen alone is a proof of concept for its ability to successfully translate "unfilmable" sci-fi literature. William Gibson, too, has been directly involved with the show's production, which also heavily favors the adaptation.

Not to mention, after its first trailer, it looks like Apple TV's Neuromancer is not bogging down William Gibson's original vision. If all goes well, the upcoming sci-fi series could become a massive hit and make up for the pitfalls and cancelation of Prime Video's The Peripheral.

Upcoming Apple TV+ sci-fi series adapting the novel Neuromancer by William Gibson, the first in his Sprawl trilogy and a foundational cyberpunk text. In it, a crew of mercenaries and a master hacker target a massive corporation with a high-stakes heist.

#3464. Why iPhone Duo wasn’t for me (but might be for you)

I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it. Here are the three main reasons why the Duo didn’t work out for me, but might for you.

I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands. You can use it one-handed, but for me it’s not nearly as comfortable as the iPhone 18 Pro. It’s too wide and too heavy to be used for long.

Perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions. But that would be a pretty significant shift for me, as there are so many situations when I don’t have both hands free.

If you already use two hands with your iPhone regularly—perhaps because you have a Pro Max model—then the Duo’s one-handed experience likely won’t bother you. But the more I used the Duo, the more I found myself missing my iPhone 18 Pro.

The biggest value proposition of a foldable is that it’s a 2-in-1 product, letting you have a standard phone but also a tablet-sized display that fits in your pocket.

I totally get the appeal, and fully expected to love that hybrid design. But after two weeks of trying, I still struggled to find times when I actually wanted to unfold the Duo. And to be clear, that’s a me problem, not an issue with the Duo itself.

I tried a bunch of apps on the inner display, and struggled to find use cases that—for me—made it worthwhile to open the Duo. But based on the feedback I’ve seen from most Duo owners, I’m very much in the minority.

I know lots of people love the Duo for video, but I don’t watch much video on my iPhone. I almost never watch YouTube, TikTok, or Instagram Reels. And for shows and movies, I stick with my TV screen and an Apple TV 4K.

Multitasking support on iPhone Duo works really well. But when I found myself needing to multitask, I still reached for my iPad Pro with Magic Keyboard attached. A keyboard-free product can’t replace my main computer (nor would I expect it to), and the Duo screen was too small to comfortably work on it.

Last year I bought an iPhone Air and absolutely loved it. Initially, the Air’s less capable camera system didn’t bother me, it was “good enough.”

After a few months though, I started missing the Pro camera system more. Then I learned that my wife was pregnant with twins, and I knew I wanted the best possible iPhone cameras to capture their early weeks and months. So I bought an iPhone 18 Pro in September.

I’ve been very impressed by iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera upgrades, and it’s great having a Telephoto lens again too. Since having the best camera system is so crucial for me right now, I knew iPhone Duo couldn’t be my only iPhone.

I initially planned to dual-carry the two models, using iPhone 18 Pro solely as a camera. But over and over I found myself wishing it was my only iPhone.

I returned mine as well. Beautiful device, but functionally not very good.

Is the iPhone Duo camera good enough for most people? Probably so. But for this year at least, with my twins aging rapidly, it’s not quite right for me. If I loved the Duo for other reasons, I would just use both models. But since I didn’t, I’m happy to stick with the iPhone 18 Pro.

In closing, I want to explicitly state that I don’t think the iPhone Duo is a bad product, and this isn’t a “bad review.”

The iPhone Duo just isn’t for me. I get the sense, though, that it’s lots of people’s favorite iPhone in years. Apple created its most unique new iPhone model since the original, and there’s plenty to love about it. I’m very curious to see how popular foldables become over time compared to slab models, because each clearly offers pros and cons. But for me, at least right now, the iPhone 18 Pro is my model of choice.

What has your iPhone Duo experience been like so far? Love it? Undecided? Let us know in the comments.

#3462. AirPods Pro 3 keep getting better, here’s what’s new in iOS 27

AirPods got a variety of new features this fall in iOS 27, several of which are exclusive to AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179). Here’s everything new.

Custom EQ is a feature that some AirPods users thought Apple would never ship, but iOS 27 adds it.

With Custom EQ, Apple now lets you set your own sound profile for AirPods. Per Apple:

AirPods are designed and engineered by Apple to faithfully represent music, TV shows and movies, and calls. If you prefer a different sound profile, you can customize how AirPods represent any audio played.

You can change the EQ by going to your AirPods’ settings ⇾ Audio & Routing ⇾ Equalizer ⇾ Custom. From here, you can adjust the sound profile for low, mid, and high frequencies.

Custom EQ is available on AirPods Pro 3, AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Max 2, AirPods 5, and AirPods 4.

Apple GymKit has been available for years, but only for Apple Watch. It lets you pair and sync workout data with compatible cardio equipment, like treadmills, ellipticals, indoor bikes, and more.

In iOS 27, GymKit expands to support iPhone using AirPods Pro 3’s heart rate sensor. My colleague Zac gave it a try:

The setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

Once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

For more details on iOS 27’s GymKit feature for AirPods Pro 3, check out Zac’s full hands-on below.

For most AirPods users, the single biggest upgrade in iOS 27 is Siri AI.

Siri AI is available on compatible iPhone hardware in iOS 27, and Apple made sure to expand full support for the AI assistant to AirPods too.

AirPods are essentially becoming an AI wearable thanks to the new Siri. It will let users do a lot more than the current Siri. Here are some key features via Apple’s website:

Earlier this year when AirTag 2 launched, Apple brought Precision Finding support to Apple Watch for the first time. Until now though, it’s been limited to AirTag 2.

But with iOS 27 and watchOS 27, Apple expands Precision Finding on the Watch to AirPods Pro 3.

AirPods Pro 3’s case includes the latest second-generation Ultra Wideband (UWB) chip, letting you find it with greater precision and step-by-step guidance right from your wrist.

With every batch of new AirPods features that debuts, the AirPods settings screen in the Settings app gets more cluttered.

But in iOS 27, Apple has a welcome fix: it’s redesigned and reorganized all AirPods settings.

Now, you’ll find AirPods settings organized into more categories and submenus, accompanied by colorful icons. It makes finding the right setting way easier and more intuitive than before.

#3460. DC's Next Batman Was Never Going To Be Nightwing

On the surface, Dick Grayson's Nightwing may seem like an obvious choice to one day succeed Batman and don the cape and cowl. After all, he was The Dark Knight's very first Robin and oldest adopted son. However, DC Comics has spent quite some time establishing a much different trajectory for Grayson, while setting up someone else entirely to one day become the next Caped Crusader.

In the past, Dick Grayson had indeed filled in as Batman in Bruce Wayne's absence. However, it's one thing to become a temporary Dark Knight or for the comics to showcase an alt-reality "What If?" type scenario (see DC K.O. Knightfight), and quite another to suggest that Nightwing will one day become a full-time Batman for the foreseeable future. That's never going to be in the cards for several reasons.

Ever since he left Robin behind, Dick's evolution into Nightwing has long been punctuated by the desire to be more than Batman and step out of his shadow. Conversely, DC Comics clearly has someone else in mind to become the next Batman, and he's already been wearing the cape and cowl: Jace Fox.

Dick Grayson has successfully taken over as Batman before, most notably after Bruce Wayne's apparent death in Final Crisis. This era saw Dick becoming a new Batman alongside Damian Wayne as his Robin in the critically acclaimed Batman and Robin run. As such, it's been proven that Dick can and has become The Dark Knight when needed (but that doesn't mean he should long-term).

When he left his role as Robin behind, Dick Grayson's decision to become Nightwing was all about creating a new identity all his own, beyond Bruce. This included his move to Gotham's sister city of Blüdhaven. In the several years that have followed, Dick has become an A-list DC hero in his own right in the modern era, leading the Titans and protecting his own city without needing Batman's name or reputation.

Perhaps even more importantly, Bruce himself has indicated that he wants something far better for his eldest son (and all his sons) than simply becoming another Batman in his stead. Likewise, Dick Grayson has retained so much more of his optimism and brightness, choosing to move past his own parents' deaths rather than Bruce and his ongoing struggle to do just that.

Rather than asking him to ever take his place full-time, Bruce Wayne has every reason to want Dick to continue being Nightwing and prove that the next generation can become something greater than Batman himself. He already knows (and has said) that Dick is a far greater hero as Nightwing than he'll ever be as Batman. As such, wanting Dick to become Batman would undermine several years of development and crucial storytelling for both characters and their relationship.

Timothy "Jace" Fox, the estranged son of Lucius Fox, is a far more interesting possibility. First introduced as the next Batman in DC's Future State initiative, Jace received a proper present-day origin in The Next Batman: Second Son, exploring his complicated history and years away from his family. When he came back to Gotham, Jace chose to take up Batman's mantle, using advanced armor to fight as a secondary Dark Knight before eventually moving to New York City.

As seen in I Am Batman, the series explored what a new character could do with the mantle of The Dark Knight outside Gotham itself. At the same time, Jace's connection to Lucius still kept him connected to many of the resources associated with Bruce Wayne's crusade.

Keeping that in mind, the upcoming Batman: Reign of Assassins series is particularly exciting. Releasing in 2027, the five-issue series reunites writer John Ridley and artist Olivier Coipel, bringing Jace and Bruce together for their first true ongoing team-up, which should no doubt provide some brand-new explorations into their dynamics as simultaneous Batmen.

All things considered, DC Comics absolutely intends to use Jace to continue examining what the Batman legacy looks like in a new generation, and it will be SO much better than Dick Grayson ever becoming a permanent next Dark Knight.

Batman: Reign of Assassins #1 is available February 27 from DC Comics

It’s an all-in-one “Dolby Atmos” soundbar — yes, that means with a built-in subwoofer. The basic model, Amazon Fire TV Soundbar, is $119, so you’re essentially paying $130 for a built-in subwoofer.

At this price point, there’s very little competition. Of course, there’s the Samsung B750F ($297, 2025 model), which has a separate subwoofer and 5.1 channels (more upfiring speakers for better surround sound). Even so, this is $50 pricier, which can be a dealbreaker if you’re on a rigid budget.

I’ve also tested the Samsung Q600F — MSRP of $499 but often on sale in the $300s — which is 2025’s model but has a 3.1.2 channel setup, which is the minimum you need for genuine Dolby Atmos. I’ll get into this more below, but that’s the long and short of it.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The Sony Bravia Theater Bar 5 is $349 with a 3.1 channel — so the same as the Amazon Plus and without the surround channels present on the Samsung Q600F — which I would recommend over the Plus if you have a little more to spare. Its separate subwoofer provides a stronger bass response without overpowering dialogue, unlike the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus.

Like the $119 Amazon Fire TV Soundbar, the Plus model also has EQ modes. These are as follows: “Music”, “Movie”, “Sports”, and “Night”. There’s also individual bass level adjustment if you want to get really particular with your listening experience.

There's a dialogue mode, but this didn't isolate speech as well as I wanted it to, especially in louder, action-heavy scenes.

Music mode (connected via Bluetooth) is fine, although the bass was a little boomy and the vocals a little too sharp. I would recommend grabbing one of the best speakers, like the JBL Flip 7, to listen to music at home.

So let’s get one thing straight: the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus does not have “true” Dolby Atmos. If a soundbar doesn’t have side-firing or up-firing channel speakers, it physically cannot project soundwaves in that way.

In Top Gun: Maverick's dogfighting scene, I could feel the soundtrack whoosh around me, and the radioed dialogue sounded as if it were coming from beside the TV

However, the Plus has “Dolby Atmos”, which means it can technically decode Atmos signals. While this obviously doesn’t produce a genuinely immersive experience, it does have its moments. In the dogfighting scene in "Top Gun: Maverick," I could feel the soundtrack whoosh around me, and the radioed dialogue sounded as if it were coming from beside the TV. As I’ll get into later, this pushed the dialogue to the back of the soundstage, resulting in me straining to hear speech.

Dolby Atmos was better in “K-Pop Demon Hunters, which is really surprising. Usually, “Top Gun: Maverick” blows other movies out of the water in terms of Atmos. Cheering crowds were louder and more immersive in “K-Pop Demon Hunters," and some dialogue was positioned well in the up-firing speakers. One character's voice was particularly crisp and immersive — the lowest female voice — which makes me think the soundbar is better at isolating lower mids than sub-bass.

Despite having a range of EQ modes and a palatable price, unfortunately, the Plus gets a 3.5-star rating from me for a reason. There's one majorly important thing holding it back.

Unlike the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar, the Plus really struggles to differentiate between dialogue and bass layers in action-heavy scenes. “Top Gun: Maverick” was particularly egregious here: Bass often overpowered dialogue, especially when the soundtrack was relatively heavy in flying scenes. I could barely hear Maverick's radioed dialogue to the characters in the control room over the string-heavy soundtrack and the flying airplane.

This was incredibly surprising, as the cheaper non-Plus model excelled in the very same scene. Bass volume was set to the minimum, and I watched on “Movie” mode.

While not as egregious in “K-Pop Demon Hunters," I still struggled to hear some dialogue. Surprisingly, the music sounded excellent in this movie, but dialogue is arguably the most important part. If you can’t hear the actors, what’s the point?

The consequences are really enormous: I struggled to make out dialogue in action-heavy scenes across the three movies I watched, which isn’t really what you want when using a soundbar. The whole purpose of a soundbar is to make dialogue more intelligible.

However, I also watched "Gilmore Girls" on basic Netflix, which sounded great. If you predominantly watch TV or YouTube, I don't think you'll notice this issue. It's just a concern for action movie buffs. In that case, I'd recommend checking out the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus with Subwoofer ($375).

At $249, the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar is incredibly affordable. There are very few soundbars that can beat this in terms of penny-per-performance.

The aforementioned Sony Bravia Theater Bar 5 is $349, so $100 more than the Amazon model, but has a dedicated subwoofer and a center channel for dialogue. I would personally save up more and buy the Sony model over the Amazon.

But if I were to save more money, I'd choose the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar (non-Plus) over the Plus version. Sure, there's no subwoofer, but it's just $119 and genuinely sounds fantastic. It's the best budget soundbar I've ever tested.

Hmm. This is a tricky one. I loved the basic Amazon Fire TV Soundbar — if you want seriously great sound at a low price, get that one. The extra $130 for the Plus model? Not worth it, if you ask me. I would either spend an extra $50 on the Samsung B750F or an extra $130 on the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus with Subwoofer.

Unfortunately, due to a lack of communication between the built-in subwoofer and the main channel speakers, dialogue can be overpowered during action-heavy scenes. Consequently, I can’t recommend this model over the Samung B750F. Personally, I would either get the cheaper Amazon Fire TV Soundbar or the aforementioned Samsung model. Or, you could save up a little extra for the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus with Subwoofer ($375) or the with Rears version ($489).

However, if you have an Amazon Fire TV and want something capable of integrating into the ecosystem seamlessly (even though you'll need a separate Fire stick or Fire TV), without having to spend an extra $50 on the B750F, the Plus is a great deal.

Tom Hanks is no stranger to a family-favorite movie. Earlier this year, he starred again in one of the best family franchises of all timeas Toy Story 5 and a fight against modern technology was unleashed on global audiences. Woody, Buzz (Tim Allen), Jessie (Joan Cusack), and the rest of the toys returned to huge success, scoring more than $1 billion at the global box office, which currently ranks as the year's third-highest-grossing film.

Unlike Toy Story 4, this fifth installment was also a big hit with critics. Hanks is a go-to voice for a family animated movie to succeed, something that happened when he joined the cast of his only feature-length Christmas film to date, voicing an impressive five characters.

The Polar Express, directed by Hanks' long-time collaborator Robert Zemeckis, was released in 2004 and has since become a festive favorite in households across the globe. However, reviewers were mixed in their initial response, criticizing the film's supposed uncanny animation, which has now been reframed as part of the film's quirky charm. The Polar Express earned $320 million at the global box office, split between a domestic haul of $196 million and a further $124 million from overseas markets, and against a reported $170 million. 22 years later, the film is a hit again as the festive season begins. At the time of writing, The Polar Express is one of the ten most-watched movies on HBO Max and has surpassed the 100-day mark on the streamer.

As The Polar Express scores big on streaming, Hanks fans can look forward to one of his most beloved '90s movies officially getting the reboot treatment. Earlier this month, Warner Bros. confirmed it was bringing back Hanks' 1998 rom-com favorite, You've Got Mail, with Jason Orley attached to direct. #3456. 10 Books Like ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’ You Should Read Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

There’s nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, Matt Dinniman’s hilarious, inventive, and surprisingly emotional book series about a man in his underwear forced to fight his way through a livestreamed game show based on dungeon-crawling video games that takes place after an alien takeover of Earth. (Did I mention he's accompanied by his ex-girlfriend’s suddenly talkative cat?)

The premise should not work, but it sure does—and it makes more sense if you know it fits into a popular genre known as "LitRPG," a blend of "literature" and "role-playing game." If you've torn through all eight books released so far and you're looking for more reads that blend surprisingly deep hilarity with tabletop and video game rules (or just similar feels), here are 10 books you should check out.

An isekai story that lands in the sweet spot for DCC fans, He Who Fights with Monsters kicks off with Jason—a completely normal, kind of boring middle manager—waking up in a strange hedge maze, completely nude (even his hair is gone). He has magic that works like a video game, and has to deal with quests that slowly give him clothes (it’s a relief when he finally acquires some pants), force him to survive cannibals, and hunt down various monsters that definitely need killing. It’s got the same “gaming rules” structure as DCC and a similarly absurdist tone, with just the right spice of darkness.

The Cradle series by Will Wight isn’t a LitRPG, and it doesn’t have Carl’s focus on humor, but it’s another progression fantasy with enough game-like elements to be a great match. Lindon is an “unsouled,” incapable of gaining any of the sacred arts and doomed to a life without a future. His lack of power makes Lindon ferociously determined to find an alternative path to power and success, and that’s what drives this story. He has to find creative ways to move forward, and slowly this leads him to a path that just might make him the most powerful person in his world. DCC fans will love the progression and the tone.

One of the key elements of any video game is the respawn—you get killed, but you pop back up to try again, sometimes at the beginning, sometimes at a save point. Django Wexler leverages that mechanic to great effect in How to Become the Dark Lord and Die Trying. Davi has been summoned to a fantasy world to be the hero, the person who defeats the Dark Lord and saves the day—but she’s failed (and died) so many times, she’s fed up, and decides that on this run through, she’s going to switch sides and become the Dark Lord, using all her knowledge gained from endless replays to her advantage. The humor is pitch-black the way DCC fans like it, and the progressive structure is a perfect fit.

Is Princess Donut your favorite part of Dungeon Crawler Carl? Of course she is. In that case, check out Andrew Seiple’s Threadbare series. Threadbare is a stuffed bear brought to magical life in a failed experiment. He’s a foot tall, full of stuffing, and extremely dumb when the story begins. But when he’s rescued by a little girl and plunged into a horrible series of dangers, Threadbare has to find a way to level up. Like DCC, Threadbare starts off leaning into the absurdity and humor, then slowly gains emotional gravitas as the story progresses.

If you play tabletop RPGs, you’ve encountered a Murderhobo or two: A character who solves all their problems by killing—even members of their own party. Luke doesn’t aspire to be a Murderhobo—he just wants to take over the family business and hang with his buddies. But when an invasion threatens the kingdom, everyone over the age of 17 is ordered to be tested for Potential. Luke’s friends all test high and join the Ascender Corps, traveling to different planes for training. Luke tests ... very low, and when he steps through a portal to engage in his training, he finds himself without any guidance or training in a strange, deadly world where his only chance of survival is to murder his way through it. It’s dark, darkly funny, and a progression fantasy like no other.

If you’re looking for a book series that combines the dark, chaotic humor, absurd game mechanics, and surprising emotional depth of Carl, here’s Ryan “Quicksave” Romano, a man who has the unique ability to literally create a save point in his existence that allows him to go back and redo things whenever he dies. Searching for a childhood friend, he becomes embroiled in a violent gang war that lets him make good use of his power—but underneath the snark and the insanity of Ryan’s existence is a surprisingly affecting story of a man who has suffered, and suffered countless tragedies that are definitely taking their toll.

If your fave bit of DCC is Carl himself—a mediocre dude in an extraordinary situation—you should read Dennis E. Taylor’s fantastic Bobiverse books. Bob is a software engineer who hits it big and promptly dies, waking up to discover a century has passed and he’s been repurposed as an AI controlling a space probe searching for new planets for humanity to inhabit. If he fails in his mission (and he’s not the only probe out there), he’ll be turned off for good. Luckily, he can make copies of himself, and he’s pretty smart. The humor here is smart and soaked in pop culture, making it a perfect match for DCC fans.

Want more of Carl’s absurdist humor? Mayor of Noobtown is the LitRPG you’re looking for. Jim dies and wakes up in a video game-esque universe and finds himself stuck in the zone designated for newbies—players with no experience, skill, or hope. The area fell out of the mainline progression mechanic a long time ago, so there doesn’t seem to be a way to gain power, and the monsters are not at all concerned about the unfairness of it all, so Jim has to figure out how to advance in a universe that seems designed to kill him (again).

If you want to lean into the meta side of things, check out Scathing Reviewer, written by an author who goes by the unusual pen name "BananaDragon." Liu Peijin is the author of a sprawling LitRPG web novel, and she’s used to the bad reviews and complaints from readers—and quite combative about it. When her books’ universe blossoms into a very dangerous new reality, she should be perfectly positioned to survive, having written the story in the first place. But her story becoming real also means her insufferable protagonist is real, and all those nasty critics are now passing judgment on her entire existence. It’s a dark, funny takedown of the entire genre itself, and DCC fans will love it.

If you want a story that parallels the dungeon crawling aspect of DCC, Andrew Rowe’s Arcane Ascension series is the ticket. The Serpent Spire is a tower of constantly changing traps, puzzles, and dangerous creatures. If you enter and survive, you emerge with magical powers. Corin Cadence’s brother entered the Serpent Spire years ago and never returned—and now Corin is determined not only to survive, but to make it to the top, where legend says a goddess will grant you whatever you wish. And what Corin wants is his brother back. It’s a literal progression combined with LitRPG rules, game-inspired puzzle-solving, and a complex magic system that fans of Carl will definitely enjoy.

#3454. Epic accuses Apple of withholding 122,000 documents, seeks daily fines

In a new filing, Epic Games accuses Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions and asks the court to impose daily fines until the company complies. Here are the details.

As a result of the lawsuit Epic Games brought against Apple in 2020, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple would have to, among other things, allow developers to direct users to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.

Apple responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them. This, in turn, led the court to find Apple in civil contempt for violating its injunction. Since then, Apple has been trying to overturn that ruling, a dispute that has now reached the Supreme Court.

At the same time, district court proceedings will determine what, if any, commission Apple may charge on purchases made through external payment links. Apple submitted its proposal on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, and Epic is expected to respond after Apple completes its document production.

In a new filing, however, Epic is accusing Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to how it arrived at its proposed commission rates.

One of the many aspects of the ever-sprawling battle between Epic Games and Apple centers on document production.

In its new filing, Epic says Apple has repeatedly failed to produce documents detailing how it arrived at its proposed commission rates, accusing the company of withholding materials it deems irrelevant to the proceedings.

Epic argues that Apple previously used questionable claims of attorney-client privilege to withhold documents during the contempt proceedings, but has now changed tactics.

Apple does introduce one tactical change from its prior campaign of delay. Whereas during the contempt proceeding Apple used bogus claims of privilege to evade its discovery obligations, this time Apple withholds thousands of documents on bogus claims of irrelevance. For example, Apple is withholding well over 99% of the documents returned by running the agreed-to search terms on the files of the four custodians Apple says decided on the proposed fee (Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Carson Oliver, and Kevan Parekh (Apple’s new CFO)) and three other key individuals (Nate Barton, Alex Roman, and Phil Schiller). Apple claims these withheld documents are not relevant to this proceeding-even though they hit on case-specific terms such as “proffer,” “contempt,” “injunction,” and “link-out.” To put this into context, while Apple produced 632 custodial documents returned by these search terms (including families), Apple is withholding over 122,000 based on a claim of non-responsiveness. Moreover, Apple claims that it completed its production from the files of these custodians, yet its production does not include a single substantive email discussing the rates Apple ultimately proposed; any notes or communications reflecting what occurred at any meeting where these rates were discussed or decided; any internal analysis of the financial or business impact of the proposed commissions; any App Store profit and loss statements; or any support for Apple’s assertion that its incremental link-out costs are “essentially zero.”

Epic goes on to state that “Apple cannot be trusted to fix this problem on its own,” proposing instead that the court order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents matching the search terms agreed upon by both parties, regardless of whether Apple considers them relevant.

Under this proposal, Apple would still be allowed to review documents for attorney-client privilege, but it would be up to Epic to determine which of the remaining documents are relevant to the case. Epic argues that existing confidentiality protections would prevent it from using any of the information for purposes unrelated to the litigation.

Given Apple’s position, Epic respectfully submits that the Court should order Apple to produce to Epic all non-privileged documents that hit on the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms, so that Epic itself can sift the wheat from the chaff. Doing so will avoid further delays and place no burden on Apple. Moreover, doing so would not raise any of the concerns that required Special Master involvement in the prior proceeding, namely concerns around the production of privileged Apple information to Epic. Under Epic’s proposed remedy, Apple would be allowed to continue its review for privilege. For these reasons, Epic asks this Court to order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents that hit on any of the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms by December 2, 2026 (one week after Apple’s deadline to substantially complete production), irrespective of any relevance or responsiveness assessment.

Finally, though Epic does not propose a specific dollar amount, it “asks that the Court impose on Apple a daily monetary sanction for each day Apple fails to comply after December 2, 2026.”

According to the court docket, a hearing on Epic’s motion was initially scheduled for November 24 before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers. However, a new order filed today, which has yet to be made public, refers the discovery dispute to a magistrate judge and includes a notice terminating deadlines and hearings.

#3452. Report: iPhone set to gain market share in 2027 amid industry-wide slump

Apple could see iPhone shipments rise 7% next year, giving it a 26% share of global smartphone shipments, according to a new report. Here are the details.

As detailed by AppleInsider, a new Morgan Stanley research report says Apple is poised to ship approximately 270 million iPhones in 2027, a 7% bump from 2026.

The forecast comes amid a change of pace for Apple, which launched only the iPhone 18 Pro models and iPhone Duo this fall, with the rest of its iPhone lineup reportedly set to arrive early next year.

Morgan Stanley notes that this could push some purchases from late 2026 into 2027, contributing to the projected shipment growth without necessarily reflecting an increase in underlying demand.

The report also comes as Apple and the rest of the smartphone industry continue to grapple with rising memory and storage prices, though previous reports have suggested that Apple is better positioned than many of its competitors to absorb those costs.

Apple raised iPhone prices in September, after keeping them stable for much of the year while competitors had already introduced price hikes. In some cases, they raised prices more than once within a matter of months.

Back to the report, it notes that global smartphone shipments are expected to drop 5% next year, compared with a previous forecast of 3.6% growth. That said, it’s still an improvement over the estimated 13.8% decline in 2026.

When it comes to Apple and the iPhone specifically, Morgan Stanley notes that consumer interest in upgrading has remained largely unchanged year over year, with 37% of iPhone owners saying they are extremely likely to upgrade within the next 12 months. That’s compared with 41% of smartphone owners overall, a figure that dropped by 2 percentage points year over year.

As for the market’s reaction to the iPhone Duo, Morgan Stanley found that 22% of non-iPhone users surveyed expressed interest in switching to Apple’s foldable device, with that figure reaching 34% in China.

Importantly, Morgan Stanley’s survey was conducted after the iPhone Duo was announced, but before it launched, so these figures reflect consumer interest rather than actual purchasing behavior.

Apple Intelligence was another factor examined in the survey, with Morgan Stanley concluding that AI features are becoming less important in driving iPhone upgrades, while factors such as battery life and upgrade eligibility are gaining importance.

Finally, Morgan Stanley found that Apple’s customer retention rate increased three percentage points to a record 93%, while its net switching rate improved to 12%.

Huawei was the only other major smartphone brand to show a positive and improving net switching rate, while Samsung and Google remained relatively neutral, and Xiaomi, Motorola, Honor, Oppo, and Vivo recorded negative rates.

#3451. Tom Hardy's 142-Minute Near-Perfect Miniseries Still Has Not Been Beaten

Two things can be true at once with Tom Hardy: he vanishes into roles with all the finesse of a deep-cover spy, and we never forget who we're watching. Such awareness isn't a negative, though; when Hardy signs his name to a project, said story arrives at our doorsteps with the rubber-stamped guarantee that he has wholeheartedly thrown himself into the character. The palpably realistic and sometimes avant-garde mannerisms, voice shifts, and physical transformations seem effortless, but audiences know the road to Hardy's results is all dedicated effort.

In 2009, right before Hardy vaulted into household name status, he left his mark on one of classic literature's most infamous, analyzed, and misrepresented figures. Emily Brontë simultaneously refined and created an archetype with Wuthering Heights, and countless riffs on Heathcliff — equal parts brooding antagonist and tragic antihero — have followed in her landmark footsteps since 1847. Every time a new movie or television adaptation rolls around, actors covet the ingeniously rich part. Many have delivered fine performances, but only a handful have gotten close enough to graze their fingertips against Wuthering Heights' stormy and tormented soul.

And while Brontë's descriptions of Heathcliff contain a degree of racial ambiguity, she inarguably establishes him as a man of color — an imperative fact that the majority of filmmakers have neglected. Without ever diminishing or excusing such consistent whitewashing, Hardy's take on Healthcliff is also one of the most definitive interpretations by far. The two-part miniseries itself remains the adaptational gold standard to date, too — desolate, macabre, bitter, thematically accurate, and feverishly intoxicating.

Wuthering Heights is a magnificently tricky puzzle to crack on the page and even more difficult to translate onto the screen. Rather than the straightforward doomed love story it has often been mistaken for, Brontë's morbid and profoundly thoughtful work uncompromisingly interrogates class hierarchy, generational trauma, domestic and systemic abuse cycles, gender and race, obsessive grief, all-consuming revenge, and psychosexual subtext.

Four love stories, four completely different ideas of what it means to be somebody's person. This is the one that matches how you actually fall, and what it would ask of you.

You do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most durable way anybody has found to do this.

You want a partner, not an audience. Somebody who wants their own life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the relationship easier.

The intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting somebody you are not supposed to want.

You do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version of it.

The 2009 limited series does justice to her vast scope, truncates little, and softens nothing. Writer Peter Bowker achieves maximum faithfulness, preserving the thematic integrity in general and by including the crucial plot beats other adaptations abandon for the sake of streamlined simplicity; eliminating the second generation of children negates Brontë's prevailing points. Bowker's scripts employ a flashback structure instead of a traditional chronological approach, which prevents the second episode from losing momentum and gives both halves equal weight.

Coky Giedroyc's direction might not contain the same level of moody lavishness as a high-budget Hollywood affair, but for 2009-era network television, the atmosphere is precisely on point. By day, the visuals luxuriate in the windswept and rocky Yorkshire Moors like the terrain is a private paradise; by night, those same locations drip with an ominous, rain-soaked, Gothic chill no warm coat or feeble lantern light can protect against. If anything, the production's subtle efficiency enables the performers to sell the emotional turbulence with maximum artistic freedom and commitment.

In a way, Heathcliff is a perfect example of Hardy both playing against type and tapping into his exact strengths. It's a demanding role, and he unearths the complete spectrum — every paradoxical layer of aching loneliness, tender desperation, wounded pride, extreme intelligence, seething spite, and punitive cruelty. A defiant survivor of abuse, ostracization, and rejection, he's understated and internalized at one moment, his eyes hollowed out by the phantoms of regret, before gliding straight into visceral rage. He can invade and dominate a room through the sheer force of his insidious physicality, yet still exert a seductively appealing gravitational pull.

The show comes from the creator of 'Peaky Blinders.'

And a Heathcliff, of course, is nothing without his beloved Cathy Earnshaw (Charlotte Riley). Another exceedingly intricate and tricky role, Riley makes Cathy as irresistible, isolated, selfish, jealous, and demanding as she should be. The woman's whims are as untethered as the wind and as dangerous as a sparking live wire; she relishes exerting control by playfully toying with her lovers. In tandem, Riley sells the overwhelming sincerity of Cathy's volatile emotions; it's readily apparent and tragic why her gilded-cage aristocratic life kills her unsatiated spirit long before it kills her body. The war between her contradictory desires — liberated freedom versus conforming to society's standards for financial security and comfort — plays across her face like an Expressionist painting.

Hardy and Riley's chemistry is so naturally thunderous that the pair married five years after filming Wuthering Heights. They capture the characters' star-crossed toxicity in all its smothering closeness, from two young and powerless outcasts who forge a home together and consume each other's chaotic passion like oxygen, to venomous snakes inflicting reciprocal misery until both parties self-destruct. Cathy and Heathcliff is no great love story by any aspirational or enviable measure. However, as terrible, damaged, and lost people who recognize their twin flame, but ruin the solace for which they yearn, they're perfect for each other — as near-perfect as this masterpiece adaptation.

#3450. Michael Connelly Finally Gives Us The Bosch Backstory We’ve Been Waiting For In New Release

This article contains mention of child abuse.

For over 30 years, Bosch has been a standout thriller series, and the author, Michael Connelly, hasn't stopped surprising readers. In his new release, Connelly delves further into the background and origin of the protagonist, Harry Bosch, than ever, shedding new light on his development.

When audiences first met Bosch in the 1992 novel, The Black Echo, Connelly introduced us to the world of the LAPD homicide detective and the cases he solves. Of course, things quickly get personal for Bosch as his background as a soldier in the Vietnam War and troubled past influence how he solves some grisly murders in Los Angeles. The Bosch TV show has done an amazing job bringing Connelly's novels to life, but it's always exciting when the writer adds texture to his backstory in the novels.

The most recent Bosch book, The Hollow, was released this past year in October 2026, and is the 26th volume in the Bosch franchise. Though Harry Bosch has come a long way since his early days solving crimes for the LAPD, Connelly keeps raising the bar, finding new ways to expand his story and crafting unbelievable thrillers that readers can't put down. Currently rated at 4.48 stars on Goodreads, The Hollow debuted to a warm reception because it takes us back to the beginning of Bosch's history.

Of course, readers know that Harry Bosch hasn't always had the easiest life, and Connelly has explored his past before, but The Hollow goes further than ever before, digging into Bosch's childhood. Just because Bosch retired from the LAPD, his time stopping criminals is far from over, and in the 2026 book, it's more emotional than ever. The Hollow touches upon Bosch's experience as a ward of the state as a child in the wake of his mother's murder.

His half-brother, Mickey Haller, tells Bosch that MacLaren Children’s Center, where Bosch suffered abuse as a child, has finally been busted in a class-action lawsuit, and Bosch is entitled to a huge settlement. However, money isn't what interests Bosch. Though he's tried to hide from this dark period of his past for a long time, Bosch is determined to solve the long-cold case of a child, Chops, he knew at MacLaren, who was found dead.

With his investigative skills and the fact that he can no longer pretend that Chops' death doesn't haunt him, Bosch has all the fuel he needs to track down the predator whom he believes killed Chops. The central villain in The Hollow is a shocking antagonist, making Bosch's investigation all the more compelling as he closes in on him. However, the most arresting part of The Hollow isn't the case, but Bosch's arc coming to grips with the abuse he faced as a child.

Harry Bosch will face something truly tragic in Michael Connelly's next Bosch book, and readers should prepare to see him in an entirely new light.

The Hollow is an emotional, intense book and one of Connelly's most cathartic, as the novel pulls no punches when it comes to bringing Bosch face to face with some of the most traumatic moments of his childhood. The Bosch franchise has always touched upon heavy themes, as Connelly's thriller novels explore dark criminal cases and murders. However, the personal element of The Hollow, and the way Bosch grows as a character throughout the story, make it a worthy addition to Connelly's work.

It makes sense that reviews of The Hollow have been positive, as it satisfies longtime fans who were hoping to get deeper insight into Bosch and his background. Though it's not the best place to start when beginning the Bosch novels, The Hollow was a vital addition to the canon and will be remembered as a pivotal volume that changed the way we see Harry Bosch forever.

#3449. WhatsApp’s first-party chat history backup service moves ahead

Select WhatsApp beta testers on iOS are now seeing an option to use the app’s own backup service as an alternative to iCloud. Here are the details.

A few months ago, WABetaInfo reported that WhatsApp was working on its own backup service as an alternative to the current method of backing up chats, which relies on Apple’s iCloud.

At the time, the feature wasn’t available even to beta testers, but WABetaInfo’s report provided details on how it would work, including 2GB of free storage, optional paid plans for larger backups, and mandatory end-to-end encryption for backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers.

Now, the site reports that some WhatsApp users running the latest TestFlight build are seeing the option to switch from iCloud to WhatsApp’s own backup service, suggesting that a wider rollout may not be too far off.

Users can switch to WhatsApp cloud storage from the Chat backup screen. Here, users will have to choose the backup provider they want to use. If they choose WhatsApp, they will have to secure their backups using end-to-end encryption. Since encryption is mandatory, users cannot skip this step. However, they can choose a different method to encrypt their backups. For example, users can secure their backups using a 64-digit encryption key. Users who do not know what to choose can opt for the passkey, which is the default method WhatsApp recommends. After users complete the setup, they can back up their chat history on WhatsApp’s servers. WhatsApp keeps the backup on its servers for four months after a subscription expires. If users do not renew their subscription, WhatsApp deletes the backup permanently.

Importantly, the site notes that backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers cannot currently be used to restore chats across platforms, meaning users switching from iPhone to Android, or vice versa, will still need to rely on WhatsApp’s built-in chat transfer feature.

Although the feature appears to be rolling out to beta testers first, the report notes that “the latest version available on the App Store is also compatible with this functionality,” meaning WhatsApp could theoretically enable it for users running the public version without requiring another app update.
