#3447. iFixit tears down Apple HomeView, finds lots of glue and endless frustration

iFixit’s teardown of the new Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair. Watch it below.

Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device.

Contrary to recent teardowns, which found significant repairability improvements with greater component modularity and easier access to internal components, the HomeView put up a fight nearly all the way through.

With heavily glued or adhesive-bonded components, including the display, speakers, antennas, and logic board, the teardown proved particularly challenging, even after the adhesive securing the display’s speakers was soaked in isopropyl alcohol.

At one point, one of them broke apart during removal, while the logic board required considerable force to separate from the chassis due to the thermal adhesive holding it in place.

iFixit’s teardown covered the two HomeView variants: the tabletop model and the wall-mounted version. Interestingly, there are some internal differences between them, as the wall-mounted model has a slightly wider logic board to accommodate capacitors that are housed in the base of the tabletop version.

As a result, the wall-mounted HomeView also has smaller internal speakers, which helps explain the differences in their audio systems that Apple had already acknowledged at launch.

Back to the tabletop model, iFixit’s teardown also showed that separating the display from the base requires either specialized tools or extensive, potentially destructive disassembly of the display assembly, thanks to the way Apple routed the connecting cables through the pivot mechanism.

Once iFixit was in the base, however, there was some good news: the USB-C port is modular and relatively easy to access, as are the passive radiators and the board powering the lower assembly.

Still, an extremely short cable connecting the woofer to the board underneath made disassembly difficult, with iFixit questioning how anyone would be able to reconnect it during reassembly.

Percentage of Apple owners who are interested in repairing their device. 0.000001%

Percentage of Apple owners who will actually try and repair their device. 0.00000001%

Given all these repairability challenges, Shahram Mokhtari joked that while iFixit doesn’t have an official repairability scorecard for this category of device, he would give the Apple HomeView a “BEEP this thing” out of 10.

#3444. Fallout 5 Official Release Update Shared By Bethesda And Microsoft

It was actually quite an exciting moment earlier this year when Bethesda finally broke cover to give us updates on basically everything they have going on right now. That meant that we finally know what's going on with Fallout, The Elder Scrolls, and even Starfield, if anyone is still invested in how that plays out in the future.

For Fallout in particular, we got a ton of exciting information, including confirmation that both Fallout 3 and Fallout: New Vegas were getting the remakes that had been rumored for a long time. In addition, Fallout 5 was also confirmed to be entering full development, though given the protracted cycles of AAA games, the crushing reality is that it's likely still a long way away from being made available to players.

Though things have been relatively quiet since, there has now been an update and it further cements exactly what we though the situation was going to be.

As first reported by GameRant, Bethesda has now reiterated to fans that Fallout 5 remains their "long-term destination," and it will likely be the last of the previously announced projects to arrive in our laps.

The story of Fallout 5 up to this point has been one of frustratingly little progress, particularly given how big the studio is. Todd Howard first spoke about the game all the way back in 2018 (now known as the cursed year), when he simply confirmed that it would be a single-player effort. He then went on to confirm that they had a one-pager for the game in 2021, before he confirmed a year later that it would be their next big project after The Elder Scrolls VI.

Back then, there would have been plenty of players out there who were expecting to be playing The Elder Scrolls VI by now, but that obviously isn't the case. In fact, it would be a major surprise if we are playing it before 2028, which likely means that Fallout 5 is going to be considerably further away, well into the 2030s.

The only potential silver lining to that timeline is that new Xbox head Asha Sharma has made it very clear that she wants Fallout to be at the center of the company's strategy moving forward. Possibly motivated by the success of the Prime Video adaptation, it may well be that additional resources are moved across to get the game out sooner.

At the same time, those remakes we mentioned earlier should also be along much sooner than that, allowing us to explore two of the better RPGs of all-time in brand-new fidelity. Though we don't have dates just yet, 2027 does seem like a reasonable estimate for the first of those, finally giving us something to do with the franchise while we wait.

At the same time, the third season of Fallout on Prime Video has wrapped filming, and that will definitely debut next year, most likely in the months around June. If that's anywhere near as good as fans are expecting, then things could be relatively positive from here on out for fans of the franchise.

Fallout is a post-apocalyptic RPG franchise set in an alternate future where a nuclear war devastates the world. Players explore vast, open worlds filled with mutants, raiders, and advanced technology. The series emphasizes player choice, allowing various approaches to combat, dialogue, and decision-making. Each game follows different protagonists navigating the wasteland to uncover secrets, form alliances, and rebuild civilization amidst the ruins of the old world. The franchise is known for its rich lore, dark humor, and retro-futuristic aesthetic, which has transferred over into its new series on Amazon Prime.

#3443. 5 Essential Classic Books for Beginners

At any given moment, Scott Simone has at least three books jockeying for his attention. He’ll never turn down a campus novel with a literary bent, nor will he hesitate to add yet another mystery to his Leaning Tower of Pisa-inspired to-be-read pile — which is built upon the bedrocks of too many short story collections, how-are-these-real true crime books, and classics waiting to be cracked open again. Topics that have him ripping through pages the fastest include closed-circle murders, unhappy professors, life-questioning philosophical deep dives, so long as they feature sharp sentences, a dark sense of humor, and at least a little malice.

He’s spent so much time in book shops over the years he is, to his wife’s chagrin, continuing to build a library that doesn’t quite respect the dimensions of the apartment meant to contain it.

If you don't want someone to read a book, tell them it’s a classic. Tell them that it changed literature. Tell them how generations of writers have tried and failed to reproduce it. Tell them no bookshelf is complete without it. Now you’ve made reading a chore. It’s homework. We seem more interested in what these books represent than what's actually between their covers. But none of that tells you whether you'll enjoy spending an afternoon with one.

And God help you if you don't enjoy one. Give up on a modern novel halfway through, and it's simply not for you. Put down a classic, and feel the judgment pour. Somebody will come along to explain what you did wrong. Perhaps you didn't understand the historical context. Maybe you missed the symbolism. Give it another go in 10 years, when you're older and a little wiser. Sometimes that's fair. But we've developed a habit of treating difficulty as a mark of greatness, as though the more you struggle through a book, the more worthwhile the experience. And that's a shame. These were novels — funny, exciting, full of people behaving appallingly — long before they became monuments to literature. And perhaps the best way to appreciate their greatness is to remember what made them worth reading in the first place.

If you think 19th-century literature is a slog, Jane Austen would like a word. And in all likelihood, it'll be a funny one. Because Austen knows how to bring the humor, especially when she's eviscerating the types of people who tend to make fools of themselves. Pride and Prejudice rotates a cast of such characters right into her firing line. There's Mrs. Bennet, who's basically willing to marry off her five daughters to whichever eligible bachelors wander into the neighborhood. There's Mr. Collins, a man so impressed with himself he has no doubt everyone else must be, too. And then there's Elizabeth Bennet, who's clever enough to recognize everyone else's shortcomings, but isn't quite so perceptive when it comes to her own. The best part: You don't need to know much about Regency England to appreciate any of this. Snobs, bores, and people who think far too highly of themselves were plentiful two centuries ago, and Austen brings them hilariously to life.

The romance is familiar enough, too. Elizabeth and the wealthy-but-insufferable Mr. Darcy spend an awful lot of time misunderstanding one another, taking offense at perfectly innocent remarks, and refusing to admit when they've been wrong. It's not so far removed from a modern romantic comedy, though there's more at stake than a few bruised egos. Money and social standing dictate much of what these people can and can't do, especially when it comes to marriage. For Elizabeth and her sisters, finding a suitable husband is as much a matter of financial security as it is romance. Yes, the language does take some getting used to, and polite society and all its rules can seem ridiculous. But Austen thought plenty of them were ridiculous, too, and she's more than happy to have a little fun at their expense.

Not every literary classic takes a fortnight to actually get going. Case in point: Around the World in Eighty Days. Jules Verne takes a simple premise, launches out of the gates with it, and never really slows his pace. Which can't exactly be said for Phileas Fogg, an English gentleman who seems a little too obsessed with punctuality. Yet he wagers £20,000 that he can travel around the globe in 80 days. This being 1872 and all, a time when travel involved nothing more than a few steamships and trains, it's an outrageous proposition. But that's all the setup Verne needs. There's no sprawling cast to keep track of and no complicated backstory to untangle. There's simply a man and a deadline — and a ridiculous number of obstacles standing between the two.

Fogg, mind you, is hardly the sort of man you'd expect to go gallivanting around the world. He's a creature of habit, so wedded to his daily routine that you'd think the slightest disruption would send him into a fit. However, Verne seems determined to test just how much the man can take. A train is missed. A connection falls through. An itinerary becomes useless. Somehow, Fogg takes it all in stride, with the composure of a man who's been told his dinner reservation has been pushed back 15 minutes. His French valet, Passepartout, isn't so accommodating, and watching him fret while his employer barely bats an eye is half the fun. And Verne makes us fret along with him. A delayed departure becomes genuinely suspenseful. Some of the novel's attitudes toward the people and places encountered along the way are decidedly of their time; but Verne's talent for turning a simple journey into one calamity after another hasn't aged much at all.

Not every difficult subject makes for a difficult book. Leo Tolstoy takes on death and regret. He delves into the despair of a life wasted in The Death of Ivan Ilyich, and he manages it in about 100 pages. The writing is surprisingly straightforward, the cast is small, and there's hardly any plot to untangle. We learn that Ivan, a Russian judge, has died before we've even had a chance to meet the man. So there's no great mystery about where this is headed. What concerns Tolstoy is how Ivan got there, and why a man who's done just about everything expected of him finds himself so unprepared for the end. It's heavy stuff, sure. But you don't need a philosophy degree or much knowledge of 19th-century Russia to understand what Tolstoy's getting at.

Tolstoy has a wicked sense of humor, which helps. Ivan's colleagues hear that he's died and immediately start calculating what it might mean for their careers. His funeral is treated as an inconvenience, something to get through before going about life. Ivan himself hasn't exactly spent his years pursuing a life of great meaning. He's been too busy climbing the social ladder and worrying about what people might think of him. Then he gets sick, and suddenly none of it seems worth much. Worse still, the people around him would sooner carry on pretending everything is fine than acknowledge what's happening to him. Tolstoy has plenty of fun exposing all this vanity and self-importance.

Toni Collette and Kit Harington are shooting a new Miss Marple and 20th Century has several more Christies in development, so the drawing room is busier than it has been in decades. Here is which of them you are, and the case for yours being the best.

Order, method, and a quiet confidence that you are the cleverest person present. Poirot is a retired Belgian police officer who solves murders by sitting still and thinking, and who is vain enough to make the reveal a performance every single time.

People tell you things because they cannot imagine you being a threat. Marple solves murders by comparing everybody to somebody she once knew in St Mary Mead, which sounds like a joke until you notice it works every time, because human beings are not as original as they think.

You have far too many ideas and roughly a fifth of them are excellent. Ariadne Oliver is a successful crime novelist who is sick of her famous foreign detective and keeps saying so, which is Christie writing about Christie and getting away with it completely.

You are steady, decent and the reason the difficult genius has anybody at all. Hastings narrates the early Poirot novels, misses most of the clues, and is the only character in the books that Poirot is unambiguously fond of, which tells you what he is really for.

You can spend eons trying to decipher Franz Kafka. Literary scholars have been at it for more than a century. But The Metamorphosis doesn't require much deciphering to enjoy. Kafka gives us the whole ridiculous premise in his opening sentence: Gregor Samsa, a traveling salesman, wakes up as an enormous insect. Gregor's reaction is almost as absurd as the transformation itself. He's worried about being late for work. He's missed his train, his boss is going to be furious, and his family needs the money. The man's no longer human, and he's fretting about how he'll explain his absence to his employer. It's horribly funny, especially because the thinking behind it isn't all that difficult to recognize.

Kafka's joke gets considerably darker as the story goes on. Gregor has spent years working to support his parents and sister, putting their needs ahead of his own. Now that he's the one who needs looking after, the family isn't exactly enthusiastic to act in kind. His sister initially takes pity on him. His father can barely stand the sight of him. Eventually, everyone gets a bit sick and tired of having an enormous insect in their house. All the while, Gregor seems more concerned about becoming a burden than he does about his own misery. It's an awful arrangement, but one that doesn't take much imagination to understand.

Nella Larsen proves you don't need a murder or mayhem for a gripping psychological thriller. She managed to do so with an old friendship and a few uncomfortable conversations. Passing is barely 150 pages, but Larsen packs enough suspicion and intrigue to fill hundreds more. It centers on two Black women, Irene Redfield and Clare Kendry, childhood friends who've taken very different paths in life. Clare passes as white, even marrying a wealthy white man who’d never guess she's Black. Odd, considering he's so viciously racist. On the other hand, Irene has built a comfortable life in Harlem, and she knows just how badly Clare's deception could end. But when the two reconnect, she can't bring herself to stay away.

There's plenty to worry about, but it's the conversations between Irene and Clare that make the novel so fraught. Larsen lets Irene do much of the interpreting for us, and we fall into the habit of taking her word for it. Clare is reckless. Clare craves attention. Clare is putting everyone at risk. And perhaps she's right about all of it. But the more we learn about Irene, the harder it becomes to separate genuine concern from jealousy and resentment. Larsen is great at making us suspicious of someone without giving us much evidence against them. So much so that an ordinary conversation can seem loaded with meaning, a perfectly innocent remark like a veiled threat. And so we find ourselves scrutinizing every little exchange, wondering who's being truthful and who's got something to hide.

Apple today announced that App Store prices for apps and In-App Purchases will be adjusted in five countries starting December 3, following changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates. Here are the details.

In a new post published on its developer portal, Apple today announced a series of changes to App Store pricing, as well as updates to tax rules affecting developers and customers in several countries, including the US.

According to the company, developers’ proceeds from eligible app and In-App Purchase sales have been adjusted in four countries, reflecting the following tax updates:

Specific to Botswana and Rwanda, Apple said that “Exhibit B of the Paid Applications Agreement will be updated to indicate that Apple collects and remits applicable taxes.”

Apple added that a new “Software as a Service (SaaS)” attribute is now available for several App Store tax categories, including App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting. Developers can review and update their tax category selections in App Store Connect.

Additionally, starting December 3, developers who rely on Apple’s automatic pricing adjustments will see changes to app and In-App Purchase prices in:

Apple usually makes these adjustments to account for changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates, and notes that prices won’t change in countries selected as the base storefront, for auto-renewable subscriptions, or in storefronts where developers manually manage their prices.

The announcement does not go into detail about how much prices will change in each country, or whether they will increase or decrease.

Finally, starting January 1, 2027, apps and In-App Purchases in the SaaS, App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting categories will become subject to sales and use taxes in California.

Apple noted that “prices on the United States storefront are displayed to customers exclusive of taxes, so the tax change will not affect them,” but added that while developers’ proceeds will remain unchanged, “the total amount customers are charged, inclusive of tax, may increase.”

Proper balance becomes crucial in your senior years

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As a certified personal trainer, I work with a wide range of clients who have lots of different fitness goals. But for my clients in their 60s and beyond, there’s usually one objective that drives their training: improving balance and stability.

I recently started working with a 60-year-old client who wanted to focus on just that. She noticed that she was a little more unsteady on her feet than she used to be, and had a few close calls with falling. After a thorough check-up with her doctor, we began our work together with the following routine.

These exercises aren’t just for seniors. It’s never too early to start thinking about your balance, so give them a try during your next workout. They’re appropriate for any fitness level and you won’t need any equipment to do them (but adding a dumbbell or two will always make things more challenging).

Check in with your doctor before trying any new workout, especially if you have balance concerns.

These exercises aren’t hard, but doing them correctly is important. Beginners should consider meeting with a personal trainer or physical therapist for feedback and guidance on form, and to get modifications if needed.

You’ll just need some room and an elevated platform, like a stair step, for this workout. Hang onto a chair or another stable surface for additional support if you need it.

Start by doing each exercise for one set of 10 reps. As your balance improves, you can add an additional set and increase your reps to 12. You can also use small dumbbells for the step-up to balance to ramp up the difficulty.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

These exercises can be done on their own or as a warm-up for other activities.

You may feel muscle fatigue when doing this workout, but you should never feel sharp pain. Stop the workout immediately and consult your physician if you feel sharp pain at any point.

The exercises in this workout force you to find equilibrium when your center of gravity is maintained over a smaller surface area – either one foot for the standing marches, step up to balance, and side step to balance, or a narrow placement of two feet for the heel-to-toe walks.

During these exercises, your deep core muscles like the rectus abdominis and internal obliques engage to stabilize and support your entire body. Your glutes and hip stabilizing muscles also work to keep the hips in a level position. The stronger these muscles are, the more conditioned they’ll be to keep you upright and sturdy during everyday movement.

Additionally, exercises like the step-up to balance strengthen key muscle groups in your lower body, like the quadriceps, hamstrings, and glutes.

#3439. 10 Shows Like 'MobLand' You Should Watch Next

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Crime dramas often attract big stars, and MobLand is no exception. The Paramount+ series stars Tom Hardy as mob fixer Harry Da Souza, with Pierce Brosnan and Paddy Considine in supporting roles and Helen Mirren having a ball as the thoroughly evil matriarch of the Harrigan crime family.

While families are complicated in even the best of circumstances, that's especially true of the Family. After you've watched the recently released second season of MobLand, try one of these other shows mixing crime and family (or Family) drama.

Theo James plays army officer Eddie Horniman (a name mentioned as often as possible), heir to the Horniman estate (there it is again) who, upon the death of his father, is named the Duke of Halstead. He learns that his dad was tied to various criminal enterprises, and that his scouse brother is millions of pounds in debt to a drug dealer. What else is the dapper, military-trained Duke to do but learn to navigate the violent underworld while looking cool? You won't be surprised to learn that this British crime drama comes from creator/writer/producer Guy Ritchie, who also has a hand in MobLand. Stream The Gentlemen on Netflix.

Another series from Taylor Sheridan (the Yellowstone guy), this pandemic-era hit stars Jeremy Renner as Mike McLusky, head of a family that’s been keeping the peace, through means fair and foul, in the title's company town for decades. The "business" of the corrupt burg happens to be incarceration, and the McLuskys thrive when business is up, even if Mike has slightly different ideas about how to run things. The show deals broadly with systemic racism and inequality in the prison system, but mostly it's a modern-day western about bringing justice to a corrupt town. It will conclude with a fifth season, streaming in 2027. Stream Mayor of Kingstown on Paramount+.

A consistently compelling combination of smart plotting and lurid sex and violence, Banshee stars Antony Starr as Sheriff Lucas Hood...kinda: He's actually a man recently released from prison who takes over that identity when the new sheriff in the small town of Banshee is killed before anyone really has a chance to get to know him. It's all part of a complicated plan to reunite with his lover Ana (Ivana Miličević), and to get back the $15 million in diamonds he lost when he went to jail—but the town is ruled over by various criminal factions, and being sheriff doesn't guarantee any kind of safety; rather, the opposite. Stream Banshee on HBO Max.

MobLand creator Ronan Bennett previously made this acclaimed series that succeeds by maintaining a narrow scope—in this case, a single London council estate. Dushane (Ashley Walters) and Sully (Kane Robinson) are residents and drug dealers at Summerhouse, maintaining an increasingly precarious grip on the criminal element in the community. Most compellingly, the series maintains an extensive supporting cast of locals both in the drug trade and impacted by it, building a disturbingly compelling world. A little confusingly, the first couple of seasons were renamed Top Boy: Summerhouse when the show moved to Netflix, so you'll want to start there before moving on to plain ol' Top Boy. Stream Top Boy: Summerhouse on Netflix.

Based loosely on a nonfiction work investigating the Mafia-like Camorra in Campania, this show focuses on the head of the Savastano clan, Pietro Savastano (Fortunato Cerlino), and his ambitious lieutenant Ciro Di Marzio (Marco D'Amore). When Pietro is arrested at the series' outset, a civil war erupts between family members and among the factions vying for control. Gone are the suits and poker games of many a mob drama—this is a brutal, street-level take on organized crime that forsakes the typical trappings of the genre. Stream Gomorrah on HBO Max.

I'm here for the Pierce Brosnan of it all, but there's also a very strong vibe match in this series that casts the one-time James Bond actor as the head of a literal crime family, even if this one's set in the American West. Adapting Philipp Meyer's 2013 Pulitzer Prize-nominated novel of the same name, the series follows Eli McCullough, a ruthless cattle baron making moves to get in on the burgeoning oil industry in the Rio Grande Valley of 1915. A parallel narrative sees Eli as a young man, kidnapped and raised among a Nʉmʉnʉʉ family. While his backstory lends the character welcome complexity, in the present, he's as determined to build his empire as he is to prepare his son and grandson to take over when he's gone. Stream The Son on Prime Video.

Tom Hardy playing a tough guy isn't terribly unexpected, but here the setting is London, just after the end of the War of 1812. Hardy plays James Delaney, who returns from Africa after ten years away (he says he'd been taken prisoner, but his story doesn't entirely add up) for the funeral of his father. Dad left nothing but a little hunk of land off of Vancouver, not worth much until the war's conclusion creates new maritime trade opportunities. Suddenly, the United States, Great Britain, and the East India Company all have eyes on the real estate, and all are willing to do whatever it takes to acquire it—and the stakes become clear once James realizes that his father's cause of death wasn't natural. Stream Taboo on Peacock and Tubi.

Best not ponder too much on the fact that this one's based on a video game, as its pedigree is only hinted at via the levels of action and violence (certainly compared to some of the other shows on this list). Colm Meaney plays Finn Wallace, the absolutely indispensable leader of London's criminal underworld, a man who's been holding everything together for decades, until his shocking murder at the outset of the series (that's not a spoiler, and we spend more time with him via flashbacks). The completely random killing by someone who had no idea what he was doing begets chaos and open violence. Finn's son Sean (Joe Cole) has been raised to take his father's place, but local, Pakistani, and Albanian gangs all move in to take control from the Finn family in the power vacuum. Stream Gangs of London on AMC+.

The great Forest Whitaker stars as the real-life Bumpy Johnson, who returned from a prison sentence to find his neighborhood falling apart and in the grip of Italian mobsters. A more than capable crime boss in his own right, Johnson resolves to take on the Genovese crime family, eventually forming a tentative alliance with Malcolm X (Nigél Thatch and, later, Jason Alan Carvell). Johnson is the lesser evil as far as Malcolm and others are concerned, and a complicated figure as both crime lord and family man with aspirations of saving his neighborhood. The show will conclude with a two-hour finale, likely airing in 2027. Stream Godfather of Harlem on Hulu.

Adopted into an Italian organized crime family as a baby, Park Joo-hyung took on the name Vincenzo Cassano, eventually becoming a mafia consigliere. After his adoptive father Don Fabio dies, Fabio’s biological son comes gunning for his brother, whom he now sees as competition. Cassano flees to Seoul, on the hunt for a secret stash of money, and in the process discovers a love interest and a new adversary in a giant business conglomerate that definitely deserves to be taken down. An incredibly popular K-drama, this one definitely puts a unique spin on the tropes of the mob genre. Stream Vincenzo on Netflix.

#3438. The UK and some other countries don’t get more Siri AI usage with iCloud+

Apple this week revealed the additional Siri AI usage you’ll get if you have an iCloud+ subscription. This ranges from doubled limits for a 200GB plan to 20 times for a 12TB plan.

However, the company’s support document reveals that some countries will not get access to these increased usage allowances …

Apple hasn’t yet specified the standard limits applicable to Siri AI usage, instead saying that these will vary depending on anything from the feature used to the overall level of demand at the time. However, it did list the proportional increases you get with paid iCloud plans.

However, tucked away in the small print in the company’s support document are some exclusions. One of them is no surprise: EU countries.

Siri AI isn’t available at all in the EU due to Apple’s perception of potential antitrust issues. Essentially, Apple believes that if it launches Siri AI there, it will be required to give competing AI services the same level of access to its devices. But three other countries are specifically excluded:

Apple gives no explanation, simply saying:

Increased access to Siri AI with iCloud+ is subject to Siri AI availability and is not available in Brazil, the EU, UK, or South Korea.

However, I have a strong suspicion about the reason.

What all three countries have in common is that they’ve taken a strong antitrust stance with Apple on a number of occasions over a range of issues.

It may be that Apple has genuine concerns about how regulators might respond if they effectively throw in free access to increased Siri AI usage. The company may fear that this would be viewed as anti-competitive by implicitly disadvantaging other AI services.

A less charitable take would be that Apple is firing a warning shot across the bows of these countries, seeking to communicate that there are consequences for what it views as attacks on its ecosystem. If customers are angered by missing out, Apple might be hoping that these feelings would be directed at regulators rather than the iPhone maker.

What’s your take? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

#3437. Anya Taylor-Joy’s Sci-Fi Thriller Is Still Her Greatest Movie 2 Years Later

Anya Taylor-Joy has brought so much to her many hits over the years, but her greatest movie is the one where she says the least. The 2024 prequel Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga sees her take over the title role from Charlize Theron and portray the early years of the post-apocalyptic warrior who became the highlight of 2015’s Mad Max: Fury Road. With George Miller’s direction and Taylor-Joy’s exceptional on-screen presence, the movie became an instant classic.

Set years before the events of Fury Road, in the radioactive wasteland of post-apocalyptic Australia, the film follows the path of Furiosa from childhood, where she is played by Alyla Browne, to early adulthood, where Taylor-Joy takes over. Stolen from her idyllic sanctuary home and forcibly adopted by warlord Dementus (Chris Hemsworth), she rises up the ranks of the Citadel, ruled by the tyrannical Immortan Joe (Lachy Hulme). She becomes caught in the middle of the rivalry between the two men, and begins using their ambition to exact revenge and work her way to freedom.

The movie is the fifth in the Mad Max franchise, but the first not to prominently feature the character of Max Rockatansky (who appears in a cameo played by Jacob Tomuri, Tom Hardy’s stunt double in Fury Road) — though many fans of the 2015 movie argue that Theron’s performance as Furiosa was the most compelling in the film, and that she was the story’s true lead. This prequel fulfills that potential with a captivating adventure worthy of its lofty predecessors.

Warning: you will cry over two different rocks.

Narratively speaking, Furiosa is an expansion of the world that was introduced in Fury Road. The 2015 film showed us the landscape passing by at 100 miles per hour, in what was essentially one big, beautiful chase movie. Max’s mission was simple – race to escape the Citadel, and then turn back to reclaim it. Furiosa’s origin story is more complex, divided into chapters and focused more on the characters involved. The torment she endures, and the loss that hardens her, are all essential to the plot, making for a much darker and more thoughtful movie.

Both are classics, but Miller’s approach is different each time. Fury Road is a practically perfect example of an action movie, with choreography and spectacle that has few equals before or since. Furiosa is an epic revenge tragedy, examining the harrowing path one must take to be compelled to overthrow tyranny. Furiosa must endure, waiting for a moment that is far in the distance, while clinging to the things that keep her soul alive. We also see more world-building, as it is revealed how the Citadel, Gas Town, and Bullet Farm interact. It is an immersive experience, different from Fury Road but brilliant in its own way.

Furiosa is a character who has learned to fly under the radar, blend into any setting, and survive at all costs. This means a character who is very careful with her words, resulting in a leading role with around 30 lines of dialogue. You might think this would be a hindrance for a star, but Taylor-Joy makes it a strength. Using everything except words, she conveys a character being molded into her environment, learning to be relentless and endure anything in the name of getting home. That means a performance that is conveyed by expression, movement, and the smallest of gestures. Great actors overcome limitations to tell stories, and the Golden Globe winner rose to the challenge.

Looking back on the film, the actor said that Miller had a very specific idea of how she should hold her face, meaning she could only use her eyes to convey emotions for large portions of the movie. “As an actor, where your job is to be able to telegraph how you’re feeling with absolutely everything at your disposal," she told GQ. "To suddenly have everything gone other than [your eyes] was quite petrifying.”

The gamble paid off, however, as she delivered a soulful, determined performance in the middle of a large-scale action thriller. There are few actors with the discipline, presence, and talent to not only take up the mantle of a beloved character, but to make it their own, and that’s exactly what Taylor-Joy does. For all the many hits of her past, and the exciting projects to come, Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga has a special place in her filmography.

#3435. Nintendo's Black Friday Deals Are Actually Pretty Good

Black Friday is nearly upon us. From now through Cyber Monday, retailers and companies alike are offering deals and discounts on their wares. While I always keep an eye out for Nintendo deals offered by stores like Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, it seems the company is offering its own discounts this year—and, surprisingly, they're actually pretty solid.

Last Thursday, Nintendo announced its Black Friday discounts. We've already seen Switch 2 sales ahead of the Black Friday season, but now, Nintendo has confirmed an official discount for the console.

Starting Nov. 22 through Dec. 5, you can pick up Nintendo's Switch 2 Mario Kart bundle for $499.99, down $50 from $549.99. That includes the console, a download of Mario Kart World, and a 90-day Nintendo Switch Online Individual Membership.

If you already have a Switch 2 console and/or Mario Kart World, you're not left out of the Black Friday deals here. From Nov. 22 through Nov. 29, Nintendo is also running discounts on several high-profile Switch and Switch 2 games:

Donkey Kong Bananza was one of Nintendo's launch titles for the Switch 2. And while it's been out for over a year, Donkey Kong's first 3D game is still among the best-reviewed titles on the console. Nintendo is taking $30 off the game's MSRP for this promotion.

Kirby Air Riders on Switch 2 is only the second installment in the series. The original launched all the way back on the GameCube, and while the title typically runs for $69.99, Nintendo is letting it go for $39.99.

Metroid Prime 4 arrived last year after an 18-year wait from Metroid Prime 3: Corruption. The game typically retails between $59.99 and $69.99 for a physical copy, but Nintendo is selling it for $39.99 during its early Black Friday promotion.

Super Mario Galaxy (both the original and the sequel) are beloved by fans. These titles originally launched on the Wii, and Nintendo rereleased both for the Switch. (The company offers a free upgrade to the Switch 2 edition.) Nintendo asks $69.99 for this combo, and while you can find it for under $60, you'll officially be able to pick it up for $39.99 before Black Friday.

Nintendo's latest Mario Party, Jamboree, has a Switch 2 edition with a rather staggering MSRP of $79.99. While it's the version of the game with the most features, it's also the most expensive. You'll be able to buy it for $39.99 for Black Friday, saving up to $40.

Nintendo rarely offers official discounts on some of its biggest titles, especially in this current era. In addition, Nintendo announced a sale on its digital store that runs from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2, though it didn't say which titles would be on sale. Just keep an eye on all these dates: The Switch 2 console promotion runs longer than the physical and digital games discounts, while the digital sale runs longer than the physical sale. Nintendo says that these discounts will be available "at select retailers," as well as its brick-and-mortar locations in New York and San Francisco. You can also buy the Switch 2 bundle through Nintendo's website.

It depends! Its Nintendo Switch 2 bundle deal runs from Nov. 22 through Dec. 5; the select games listed above will be on sale from Nov. 22 through Nov. 29; and digital titles will have discounts from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2.

While we don't know which digital titles will be discounted yet, we do know that physical copies of Donkey Kong Bananza, Kirby Air Riders, Metroid Prime 4: Beyond, Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2, and Super Mario Party: Jamboree will be on sale for $39.99 each.

Yes! The Switch 2 alone costs $499.99, so you essentially get the game for free. Mario Kart World is also one of the console's best multiplayer titles right now, so it makes sense to pick it up in this bundle.

'Roman J. Israel' might be the best Denzel performance you've never seen

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Verdict: If I were just judging Denzel Washington's performance, I'd probably give "Roman J. Israel, Esq." five out of five stars. Unfortunately, I have to grade the movie as a whole. Outside of Denzel's Oscar-nominated portrayal of the titular attorney, there's not much going for this legal thriller, which masquerades as a dramatic character study until its final act. It's still worth watching, but only just.

Where to watch: Stream "Roman J. Israel, Esq." for free on Pluto TV

Like most people, I have never seen "Roman J. Israel, Esq." I knew it would eventually come up in the Denzel Watchathon, but until recently, it was just a name on a list of movies to watch; presumably just an unremarkable piece of Denzel's impressive filmography.

But then something happened — I started getting fed clips from this movie on TikTok. Was the Chinese government spying on me, knowing that this movie was approaching in my 52-film journey through Denzel's career and trying to pique my interest? For legal reasons, I certainly can't claim that to be the case, but regardless of why these clips were suddenly in my algorithm, one thing was clear to me: Denzel is really good in this movie.

Turns out, I'm not the only person who got that impression, because the legendary actor was nominated for his eighth Oscar for his portrayal of the titular attorney.

However, that's essentially where the praise for this movie ends. Despite featuring future Oscar nominee Colin Farrell alongside Denzel, and a screenplay written by director Dan Gilroy (who, while not as accomplished as his brother Tony, has still written and directed some great movies), this movie fell flat critically and commercially. It is currently rated 55% fresh by critics on Rotten Tomatoes. Audiences don't rate it much higher; just 57%. It brought in just $13 million on a $22 million budget, making it an undeniable flop despite featuring an award-worthy performance from Washington.

So with that knowledge in mind, I was ready to judge the movie for myself. Were the TikTok clips foreshadowing an excellent movie to come? Would I soon join the group of people underwhelmed by this film? Two hours later (plus some commercials), I had a definitive answer.

If you want to watch this movie before you read on, I have good news! It's currently streaming for free on Pluto TV, one of the best free streaming services we've tested.

Malcolm has been with the Streaming team at Tom's Guide since 2023, reviewing dozens of movies each year so you don't have to watch the bad ones.

As already mentioned, "Roman J. Israel, Esq." stars Denzel Washington as the titular character. Roman is a partner at a small criminal defense firm in Los Angeles until, suddenly, his partner, William Jackson, has a heart attack and goes into a permanent coma. That leads Jackson's estate to bring in big-shot lawyer George Pierce (Colin Farrell), one of Jackson's former law students, to help wind down the firm's operations, as it turns out the partnership has been hemorrhaging money, unbeknownst to Roman.

Here are some of the other Denzel Washington movies I've covered to date in my Denzel Watchathon:

Read more: Every Denzel Watchathon movie so far

Roman isn't left looking for a job long, though. Pierce offers Roman a job at Pierce's firm, seeing Roman's clear talent as a legal mind. However, Roman quickly clashes with the culture at his new firm, and it's obvious why.

To be on the safe side, I'll describe Roman as a ... socially awkward character, but I think most people today would identify him as neurodivergent. He's a brilliant analyst of the law. His research is impeccable. But he has zero people skills and strong moral and ethical convictions that often lead him to butt heads with basically everyone he has a conversation with.

This forces Denzel to give a fairly uncharacteristic and complex performance. While Roman shares Denzel's proclivity for effortlessly spewing compelling dialogue, there's none of the gravitas that comes with Washington's more verbose, award-nominated performances. Roman has a well-educated, well-spoken tongue, but he doesn't have the smooth, silver tongue of someone like Alonzo in "Training Day," or even historical figures Malcolm X and Rubin "The Hurricane" Carter.

There's also a physical element to the performance. It's unclear whether he's wearing a relatively subtle fat suit, bulkier clothing, gained actual weight for the performance or some combination of the three, but Denzel as Roman is a noticeably larger figure than I typically associate with the actor. Not that he's ever diminutive on screen; he's as often an action star as he is a dramatic force of nature and typically he's in excellent shape. But the physique of Roman is one I'd associate more with Forest Whitaker than Denzel. In fact, I couldn't help but think about what the movie would be like with Whitaker, an incredible actor in his own right, as Roman instead of Washington.

For most of the movie, you'd be forgiven for fast-forwarding through every moment that isn't Denzel talking. The TikTok clips I mentioned in the introduction of this review? They're probably 90% of this movie that's worth watching. That is, until we get to the third act, when this legal thriller actually becomes ... well, thrilling.

Perhaps it's for the best that Denzel got the role, though, because it's essentially the movie's sole saving grace. Farrell isn't miscast, but he's woefully underutilized as Pierce, and it's not the most emotive performance, save for a few moments. Roman's love interest, Maya (Carmen Ejogo), has zero chemistry with Roman. It's awkward from beginning to end, and you almost want to fast-forward through their scenes together.

In fact, for most of the movie, you'd be forgiven for fast-forwarding through every moment that isn't Denzel talking. The TikTok clips I mentioned in the introduction of this review? They're probably 90% of this movie that's worth watching. That is, until we get to the third act, when this legal thriller actually becomes ... well, thrilling.

I don't want to spoil the twist that ultimately thrusts this legal thriller into its propulsive, paranoid conclusion. But I will say that Roman, normally so strong in his convictions, finally reaches a breaking point, and it's the first time in the movie that the character becomes interesting rather than merely a vehicle for impressive dialogue.

I realize that I've spent a few paragraphs talking about this film's lowlights, but despite its flaws, it's still a movie I recommend watching for anyone who loves a great Denzel performance. While the movie is far from the best he's ever been in, his performance is well-deserving of the Oscar nomination it earned. Now that I've seen it for myself, I'll freely admit that it's a quintessential part of his oeuvre and certainly merits inclusion on his highlight reel.

#3433. Banks, FAA, Microsoft, Apple – no systemic attack on the US, says White House

A set of major tech outages in close succession is leading some to speculate that they are connected, and that the US is under systemic attack by a hostile state.

All the evidence suggests otherwise, with individual explanations for each of them – and the White House is now saying as much in a bid to put fears to rest …

Whether there was or wasn't a cyber attack, I wouldn't believe a single word from the White House.

On Thursday, a widespread Microsoft 365 outage ran into the following day when two unrelated issues coincided. Friday saw a nationwide ground stop of US air traffic due to a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centers. On Monday, a bug in a Chase bank system saw disruption not only to the bank itself, but also other banks where Chase was a party to a transaction. Finally, yesterday saw many Apple services offline, with retail stores also affected.

The Apple outage doesn’t appear to have been significant enough to have reached the administration’s radar, but CBS News reports secretary of state Marco Rubio saying the others are unrelated.

“The Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago. These issues that we’ve seen from a technical standpoint are completely unrelated one from another,” Rubio said […]

“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind. Each of them are distinct, and they’re different in their causation.”

The statement was backed by Senator Mark Warner.

Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, also said on Tuesday that there’s no indication these incidents are the result of an attack.

Warner went on to say that the ability of AI systems to find vulnerabilities at “unprecedented speed” does, however, mean companies and government agencies alike need to be ready to patch vulnerabilities immediately.

#3430. 6 Intense War Films of the 2010s, Ranked by Rotten Tomatoes Score

Ben Brewster is a filmmaker, critic, screenwriter, and actor whose work sits at the intersection of film culture, craft analysis, and storytelling.

He is a movie list contributing writer at Collider and a contributing writer for High on Films, where he covers contemporary cinema, independent film, and festival releases with an eye toward narrative structure, performance, and visual language.

Ben is an active film festival participant, having worked with Newport Film, the Nantucket Film Festival and as a screener for the Austin, Boston & Woodstock film festivals.  He brings to that work a programming instinct shaped by years of close engagement with independent and documentary cinema. This comes with a deep investment in the kinds of films that rarely find their way into the mainstream conversation without someone willing to advocate for them.

His background spans documentary and narrative filmmaking, film marketing, and production, including work with award-winning directors. This as well as developing his own indie production company, Lilac Creative Studio, through which he develops and produces original work across fiction and nonfiction forms.  His debut documentary, Diamond in the Rust, is an examination of economic redevelopment and displacement in the Queens area of New York City. The film was recently accepted to the Unisphere Film Festival, the Defense of Democracy Film Festival, and the Urbanite Arts & Film Festival. This would mark his first festival recognition as a director.  In addition to his writing and programming work, Ben hosts Beneath the Bloom, a film podcast exploring the work behind the scenes in cinema, and the struggles one can face to make a movie become a reality. The show reflects the same sensibility that runs through all of his work. A conviction that film is not merely entertainment but one of the most powerful tools human beings have for understanding each other.

Across mediums, his work is driven by a deep belief in film as a communal, transformative art form.

In the 2010s, war films felt odd and hard to pin down. The fighting in Iraq and Afghanistan was still running its course. At the same time, World War II veterans were passing away one by one. Hollywood looked two ways in response. It nodded back to the older "good war" stories that shaped the genre for years. It also faced newer conflicts that did not end neatly. No clear heroes always showed up. Because of that, many movies seemed to argue with each other about what a war film is supposed to do and what it is supposed to stand for in this decade.

The top films from that era share one main trait: intensity. This was the period of films that try to place you right in the middle of events. Directors like Christopher Nolan and Sam Mendes leaned into big, crisp images and shots that do not cut away for a long time. The goal was simple, even if the work was not. Put the viewer in the mud and the water. Other filmmakers, including Kathryn Bigelow and Peter Berg, leaned toward a documentary kind of drive. Their stories often felt like they came straight from headlines. Even the sound mattered a lot. In several cases, major awards recognized the way these films made gunshots, machinery and quiet hit hard in the gut.

Some movies in this list got mixed reviews from critics. A few of the highest earners also stirred strong reactions. This happened most often when the films dealt with tense recent history. If you sort them by Rotten Tomatoes scores, you get a quick, not necessarily wholistic view of what some critics thought at the time. That method is by no means perfect. Scores do not always say how a film has held up later. They also do not always match what viewers liked. The range here is wide. There are grim POW survival stories. There are also very detailed retellings of real military missions, scene by scene. These are the most intense war films of the decade, ranked.

Angelina Jolie directed Unbroken, based on Laura Hillenbrand's 2010 book about Olympic runner and bombardier Louis Zamperini. The film stars Jack O'Connell as Zamperini, who survives a plane crash in the Pacific. He drifts on a raft for 47 days before being captured and taken away by the Japanese. O'Connell plays him with a wiry, stubborn energy, with Jolie cutting between flashbacks to his boyhood and his running days in between the horrors. He lands in prison camps under the cruel corporal Watanabe (Miyavi), known as the Bird, who runs the prison camp. The great Roger Deakins captured the open ocean and shot the muddy camps in wide, painterly-like frames.

Joel and Ethan Coen, Richard LaGravenese, and William Nicholson share the screenplay credit. Unbroken opened on Christmas Day 2014 and grossed $163 million worldwide. Rotten Tomatoes lists Unbroken at 52%, and its consensus calls it well-intentioned but too dependent on overly familiar prestige war genre beats. Deakins earned an Oscar nomination for his cinematography, and the National Board of Review named the film one of its top ten of the year, despite the Oscar bait it had written all over it. Many felt the story became a long parade of suffering, although the audience score was friendly, landing at 70%. Zamperini died in July 2014, a few months before it opened, and a faith-based sequel, Unbroken: Path to Redemption, followed in 2018.

A drawl, a fedora, and a killer robot walk into Hollywood.

Clint Eastwood directed American Sniper at age 84. It is a biopic of Navy SEAL Chris Kyle, the most lethal sniper in U.S. military history. He's a Texas cowboy who netted the nickname Legend for his pinpoint accuracy in Iraq. Bradley Cooper bulked up for the role, and plays Kyle across four tours in Iraq, as he struggles to connect with his wife at home, Taya (Siena Miller). Jason Hall adapted the script directly from Kyle's memoir, with the film cutting from Iraqi rooftops to quiet kitchen scenes in Texas. Rotten Tomatoes lists it at 71% from critics and 84% from audiences, and moviegoers gave it an A+ CinemaScore.

The opening scene, in which Kyle must decide whether to fire at a child carrying a grenade, sets a tense tone. A rival sniper known as Mustafa gives the story a cat and mouse thread. Cooper earned a Best Actor nomination, one of six Oscar nominations that included Best Picture and a win for Sound Editing. American Sniper grossed $547.6 million worldwide on a $58 million budget, marking it as Eastwood's highest grossing film, and the biggest January release ever up to that point. Controversy followed, with critics arguing about its heroic portrait of Kyle and its historical liberties. More than a decade later, it landed in Netflix's top 10 with 4.4 million views in a single week.

David Ayer wrote and directed Fury, which follows a five-man Sherman tank crew pushing through Germany in April 1945. It's when the war's last days are its most brutal, and Brad Pitt plays Wardaddy, a battle-scarred sergeant who has kept his crew alive since North Africa. Logan Lerman is Norman Ellison, a young typist forced into the crew, with Shia LaBeouf, Michael Peña, and Jon Bernthal as the veterans who both mock and protect him. Ayer allegedly put the cast through a brutal boot camp before filming.

Fury grossed $211.8 million and opened at No.1 at the box office on a budget of about $68 million. The production used a real Tiger tank, Tiger 131, the only operational Tiger in the world. Rotten Tomatoes lists it at 75% from critics, and 84% from audiences. The consensus calls it a well acted, raw depiction of war that does not fully live up to its lofty ambitions. James Berardinelli praised how it shows the horrors of war without reveling in cruelty, while LA Weekly's Amy Nicholson felt that Ayer wallowed in ugliness. Ayer drew on the real 2nd Armored Division, nicknamed Hell on Wheels.

1917 follows two young British soldiers on a single day in April 1917, and Sam Mendes built it to look like one unbroken shot. George MacKay and Dean-Charles Chapman play Lance Corporals Schofield and Blake, two young British soldiers sent across no man's land to deliver a message that could save 1,600 men from a German trap. Mendes co-wrote the story with Krysty Wilson-Cairns, drawing on tales his grandfather Alfred Mendes told him about WWI.

Roger Deakins shot through trenches, craters, and rivers, and captured a burning town without a visible cut. Colin Firth, Benedict Cumberbatch, Mark Strong, and Andrew Scott appear in brief but memorable roles. Rotten Tomatoes lists 1917 at 88% from 472 reviews, and its consensus calls it hard-hitting, immersive and an impressive technical achievement. The movie won three Oscars, garnering a Best Picture nomination as well. It also took home the BAFTA for Best Film and the Golden Globes for Best Motion Picture, Drama and Best Director. The night sequence in a burning town lit by flares and the final run across the battlefield are the most visually stunning sequences.

Zero Dark Thirty opens with darkness and the sound of real 9/11 calls. Kathryn Bigelow directed the film off a script from Mark Boal, her collaborator on The Hurt Locker. Bigelow constantly stresses the stakes, with Jessica Chastain as the lead Maya, a CIA analyst whose obsession has driven a decade's worth of work hunting Osama bin Laden. The film then pivots to harsh and brutal interrogation scenes, with Jason Clarke playing the interrogator Dan, and Jennifer Ehle, Kyle Chandler, Mark Strong, and Joel Edgerton rounding out the cast.

Rotten Tomatoes lists it at 91% from 304 reviews, with an 80% audience score. Boal's script moves like a procedural, with offices, briefings, and dead ends. Critics called it gripping, suspenseful, and brilliantly crafted. Chastain earned an Oscar nomination for Best Actress, and the movie tied with Skyfall for Best Sound Editing. The final 30 minutes recreate the May 2011 raid on the Abbottabad compound in dim green night vision, and the sequence is considered among the most tense in modern war movies. Controversy surrounding its torture scenes has never faded, and some critics now see the movie differently after the 2014 torture report.

Dunkirk divides its story into three timelines, one week on the beach, one day at sea, and one hour in the air. Christopher Nolan depicts the 1940 evacuation of Allied troops through the perspective of Tommy (Fionn Whitehead), a young solider hunting for any way off the sand, and Harrier (Tom Hardy), a spitfire pilot with a failing fuel gauge. Mark Rylance is a man named Mr. Dawson, a civilian who sails his boat across the channel to help rescue troops. Kenneth Branagh, Cillian Murphy, Harry Styles, Barry Keoghan and Jack Lowden appear in the ensemble. Hoyte van Hoytema shot it in large format, and Hans Zimmer's score keeps a ticking clock running in the background.

Rotten Tomatoes lists Dunkirk at 92%, with an 81% audience score. Nolan used real ships and planes which gave the beaches and skies a physical weight. The consensus describes the project as an emotionally satisfying spectacle from a writer-director in full command of his craft. Dunkirk grossed more than $500 million worldwide and saw eight Oscar nominations, including Best Picture and Best Director. Between the grand practical effects, the dialogue is sparse, and the sound design carries much of the tension. Critics have called it one of the most immersive war movies ever and one of the best movies of the 2010s.

#3429. MacPaw’s Moonlock comes to iPhone, helping users detect potential scams

After launching Moonlock for Mac last year, MacPaw is bringing its scam-detection app to iPhone today. Here are the details.

When MacPaw launched Moonlock on the Mac, the company described its new app as something that “complements Apple’s built-in security tools, protects from Mac-specific malware, and helps you understand cybersecurity better.”

In practice, the Mac app includes real-time protection against potential threats. Users can also manually scan their Mac for malware, including suspicious files hidden in system folders and email attachments.

Beyond that, Moonlock includes a VPN to encrypt internet traffic, a network inspector that shows where apps are sending data and lets users block connections to specific countries, and an AI-powered scam detector that analyzes messages pasted into the app for signs of phishing. It also helps users review and adjust macOS security settings.

Today, MacPaw is launching Moonlock for iPhone, a move the company says “helps people recognize potential scams, understand their iPhone’s security and take practical steps to improve it.”

Unlike the Mac version, Moonlock for iPhone doesn’t scan for malware, as iOS prevents third-party apps from accessing other apps and their files. Instead, it focuses on identifying potential scams, checking for exposed personal information, and helping users improve their iPhone’s security.

On the iPhone, Moonlock lets users quickly check suspicious texts, screenshots, and QR codes for phishing, in addition to checking whether their email addresses have appeared in known data breaches.

As MacPaw explains it, Moonlock’s Scam Detect “helps people check suspicious messages they encounter throughout the day. Whether it’s a text message, a screenshot shared by a friend, or a QR code, users can paste, scan or share content directly with Moonlock and receive an assessment explaining why something may be suspicious.”

Here’s Oleg Stukalenko, Head of Product Management at Moonlock by MacPaw, on today’s launch:

“When we launched Moonlock, our goal was to make cybersecurity something anyone could understand and use. But so much of what people do today, from banking to everyday conversations, happens on their phones. Bringing Moonlock to iPhone felt like the natural next step. We want to help people spot a scam before they tap, see where their security stands, and know exactly what to do next.”

MacPaw adds that Moonlock for iPhone also includes the following features:

MacPaw’s Moonlock for iPhone is free to download, with subscriptions available for $9.99 per month or $49.99 per year.

#3424. Trump Administration Releases Files On 'Bigfoot'

The Trump administration is releasing government files on the age-old debate over the existence of the mysterious Bigfoot -- and you might just be surprised with the findings from a biologist.

Here's the deal ... The United States Forest Service has released 3 files under the title, “Bigfoot/Sasquatch Records," detailing efforts by the US government to determine if Bigfoot is a real Sasquatch stomping around the Pacific Northwest and North American forests or just some jokester in a costume.

In 1982, Rodney L. Johnson -- a biologist -- was recruited by the US Department of Agriculture to examine 3 locations containing large footprints purportedly belonging to Bigfoot in a wooded area of Washington state. Johnson subsequently wrote a 6-page memo for the USDA, in which he reported his findings.

Johnson wrote that he discovered footprints mostly on muddy trails in Umatilla National Forest and photographed the tracks from "Site A," "Site B," and "Site C." You can see it all in Johnson's memo released by the US Forest Service right here.

Ultimately, Johnson concluded that the tracks he examined at Site A and Site B were made by "something other than a 300-pound plus two-footed being." Johnson also wrote that "if the tracks were faked, someone went to a great deal of trouble and detail."

He added that the "print" marks on the foot would have to be very hard to duplicate," and "they appear very natural." Furthermore, Johnson wrote, "I would almost suspect a cast made of an actual foot would have had to be used to make the 'fake' feet. If this were the case, though, the other creases in the foot should have shown."

Finally, Johnson wrote that Site C contained 12 tracks in a dry open area and the prints were similar to those found at Site A and Site B.

In a nutshell, Johnson didn't crack the case for us ... it's still a mystery whether the huge furry, mythical figure is real or not ... but he did provide some expert opinions that bring us closer to the answer.

#3421. The Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess adds new color grading sets, expands to iPhone

VWFNDR + MBL, an Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess and delivers high-quality DNG (RAW) files, is getting a 2.0 release with improved color grading and an expansion to the iPhone.

VWFNDR + MBL launched on Android in May 2026 with a few points that stood out. A unique UI that adapts to the shot, minimal processing for a natural look, and support for DNG files at a level that only Google’s Pixel Camera app can truly compete with.

The app has been downloaded over 300,000 times since then, and is now getting a pretty substantial update.

On Android, this comes in the form of new color grading profiles built into the app. “NATURAL,” “NIHON,” or “B+W.” The app still saves an unprocessed DNG alongside the JPG and the grading adapts across the frame rather than having a fixed result, keeping highlights and shadows in place.

Colour grades: MBL still records unprocessed Bayer RAW DNG, and the JPG it renders alongside now uses one of three grades: NATURAL, NIHON, or B+W. Grading happens on VWFNDR’s own spatial engine. Instead of applying a fixed LUT, it adapts across the frame, much like a raw editor, so highlights and shadows keep their detail. The DNG stays untouched.

The rest of VWFNDR + MBL 2.0 takes place off of Android.

In a rare case of the tables turning, MBL was released first on Android, and only on Android for the first several months. But VWFNDR is now bringing the app to iPhone with support for variable aperture on iPhone 18 Pro and Content Credentials, Apple’s version of the C2PA standard that’s meant to prove a photo is real and not AI-generated.

#3420. 'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

In all the years you've been online, you've likely created more accounts than you can remember, whether to shop on a website you made one purchase from, sign up for a newsletter you've since stopped reading, or download apps for school or work that you no longer need.

These so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's important to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

You're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that company or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

Unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

The next place to look is in your email: Search for account confirmation and verification emails as well as password resets using keywords like "verify your email," "free trial," "welcome," "confirm your account," or "sign up." Add a date filter to narrow down older accounts. Do this across all of your email addresses.

Once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, update the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

I have many gripes with modern smartphones, but one of the things that really grinds my gears is the trend of Godzilla-sized camera bumps on the backs of phones, Apple's doing it, Samsung' seems to be planning on it, and a lot of Chinese brands look like they've been hit by a rogue hockey puck. I've been testing the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, which also has a large, iPhone-looking camera bump, but this time things are different.

Xiaomi has taken on the task of making the most out of that normally-wasted space on the camera bump by turning it into a screen. This is not the first phone to feature a rear-mounted screen, or even the first Xiaomi flagship to do so, but in a world of phones that all seem to feel and look the same, it's quite exciting to see a phone company offer something that helps its phones stand out.

But the question is not whether the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's Back Display is interesting, it's whether it's able to justify its own existence.

Looking at the 18 Pro Max, my mind immediately jumped to the cover displays on compact foldables. The way the display wraps around the two main cameras is reminiscent of the Galaxy Z Flip 8 and the Motorola Razr. It's a little smaller than those screens, measuring 2.9-inches compared to those 4+-inch screens, but all three share a common purpose.

This is a way to use your phone without actually using your phone, using the smaller screen to look at basic information like the time or notifications on a smaller and more power-efficient display. At the same time, and as Xiaomi is keen to emphasize, it's a way to customize the look and feel of your phone in a way that cases and other accessories just can't manage.

My initial thoughts upon looking at the back of the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max and playing around with the screen weren't totally positive. I couldn't stop comparing it to the cover screens on foldable phones, and the fact that those screens are front-and-center when you take out your device. Xiaomi's screen is on the back, which is not part of my phone I tend to pay very much attention to.

But the more I used it, and the more I figured out that it wasn't just a glorified clock and notification alert, the more I realized that my initial reaction was the wrong way of looking at things.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The idea that this is potentially a very valuable feature clicked when I opened up the camera on the Back Display. This allows you to take selfies using the main cameras, in a similar fashion to foldable phones, using the rear-mounted screen as a viewfinder. This means you're taking selfies with the 200MP main camera, rather than the lower resolution hole-punch camera on the front.

I'm not going to lie, though. This isn't a fully-fledged phone screen capable of running all the apps and services that you've got installed. It is significantly more limited than that, and the difference is like describing the difference between a smart home hub and a tablet.

The home hub may be useful for its own specific use case, but it doesn't have the same versatility or usefulness as a tablet running Android or iPadOS.

The Back Display is great for glancing at notifications and the time, especially if you tend to leave your phone lying face down. It even supports Live Activities on a handful of apps, including letting you control music playback on Spotify. Plus, it's possible to customize your screen with different backgrounds and clockfaces, depending on what your own personal tastes and style might be.

So far so good, though I can't say that I've ever felt using my main screen for those tasks has ever been a particular burden — especially since I'm just not used to looking at the back of my phone.

Then again, if you already have a smartwatch, that's not going to mean much, since you already have the bulk of this information available on your wrist.

Xiaomi does seem to be hinging on Generative AI to turn this screen from a gimmick into something you'll want to use throughout the day, thanks to a built-in system that lets you vibe code your own apps.

Anyone that remembers the flop that was Windows Phone will know that success of a mobile platform hinges on app support. Your apps give the system value, and without developers actively contributing to an app store, there's little reason for people to actually invest in one of your devices.

So how do you get app developers on board to add utility to a niche display on the back of a handful of phones? You don't. You hand that job to the users, and let generative AI do all the hard work. So Xiaomi added a prompt-based system for creating Back Display apps from scratch, as well as an App Store of sorts that lets you see a curated selection of what other people have created.

Options I can see include workout schedules, mini games, educational tools, timers, and all kinds of different options, though I have no idea how effective or accurate they actually are compared to full-coded apps. Still, it's nice to see that there's a way to improve the usefulness of the Back Display — even if it would be nice to have proper Android apps on offer.

I found that basic prompts did work, but the more detail you could offer the better the outcome. Xiaomi can "polish" your prompt to better your chances of generating a usable app.

However, this does not guarantee that the app would successfully generate — or that it would work. It took me multiple attempts to create a Doom clone, and even when it did, I kept getting killed off by a monster hiding out of my line of sight.

So it's not quite as painless as having a developer-made app, and playing games on a small screen isn't ideal. But in the absence of additional features, this system is fairly good at filling that niche.

I've spent my entire life looking at the front of my phone, and never really concerning myself with what's on the back. Even in the pre-smartphone era the screen was everything, whereas the back was just... not important. If rear screens start to take off, that could change the way people interact with their phones in a big way. And that's obviously going to take a lot of getting used to.

That's probably the biggest hurdle these rear screens will face. There's certainly no shortage of utility, especially with the generative AI apps. It's just reprogramming user habits to glance at the back of the phone rather than looking at their main display. It's going to be an uphill battle to convince people that these screens are worth it, especially when they have to compete with wearables.

If it weren't for the AI apps I'd say these screens don't have much of a chance. I'm not convinced that they will take off, aside from a few niche gimmicks, but at least they have some sort of unique selling point to work with.

We’re expecting Apple to use a combination of ultra-thin bezels and curved glass to create the illusion of no bezels at all – a more sophisticated version of the effect seen on the Apple Watch. Today’s report says the bezels are around 1mm thick.

The curved edges on the quad-curved version are approximately 1mm wide. However, because the glass curves around all sides, when viewed straight on from the front, the bezel becomes nearly invisible, creating a near‑borderless appearance. The actual visual effect could be quite stunning.

We yesterday saw an AI-generated render of what the design could look like. It’s expected to be the biggest redesign of the standard iPhone since the iPhone X.
