#3415. Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

To rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

It's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

This big-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and company also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

Alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley shows up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

Mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

There's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime

I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

It doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

The animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

This BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

The current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”

A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

#3414. 5 Thriller Movies We Actually Want To See a Remake Of

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

Remakes have a bad reputation, and unfortunately, most of the time, they have earned it. The problem is that studios love banking on famous titles and hoping nostalgia will do the heavy lifting. That doesn’t really work with the thriller genre, where the whole experience depends on not knowing what happens next. Once audiences know the twist, there is very little reason to sit through the same story again.

A straight copy of a classic thriller has almost no suspense left to offer. This means that the thrillers that are actually worth remaking are a little different. They’re the ones with brilliant setups that were either held back by their era or were way ahead of their time, with their fears feeling more real today than ever before. Here is a list of five thriller movies people actually want to see remade, as long as they have the right filmmakers behind them.

Dead Calm is a thriller that only needs three people and a lot of open water. The film follows Nicole Kidman and Sam Neill as Rae and John Ingram, a married couple who set out on a long sailing trip across the Pacific to grieve after their young son is killed in a car accident. Out in the middle of nowhere, they spot a man named Hughie (Billy Zane) frantically rowing away from a sinking ship. Hughie claims that the rest of his crew died of food poisoning, but when John rows over to investigate, the bodies he discovers tell a very different story. By then, Hughie has taken off in the couple’s yacht, and Rae is trapped aboard with him.

The best thing about Dead Calm is how simple it is. The film is a cat-and-mouse game with nowhere to run and nobody coming to help. What’s even better is that director Phillip Noyce squeezes every bit of tension out of this narrative. That complexity makes it a natural fit for a modern remake. A new version would just need to deal with the fact that satellite phones and GPS make getting stranded at sea much harder today, which could actually add an interesting twist to the story. All a Dead Calm remake needs is a smart director and two strong leads to become the kind of adrenaline-fueled, nerve-wracking thriller that has been missing from the big screen for a while now.

Brian De Palma’s Blow Out bombed at the box office when it first came out, but it has since been recognized as one of the greatest conspiracy thrillers ever made. The film stars John Travolta as sound-effects technician Jack Terry, who works on cheap slasher movies. One night, while recording sounds in a park, Jack captures a car swerving off a bridge and into the river. He manages to rescue a young woman named Sally (Nancy Allen) from the wreck, but the man driving, a governor who was planning to run for president, is killed. When Jack plays back his tape, he hears something that sounds like a gunshot right before the tire blows out, and he soon realizes he has recorded a murder that powerful people want covered up.

Blow Out is a thriller story about how easily the truth can be buried, and that idea feels even more relevant now. In 1981, Jack’s audio tape was the only proof that something was wrong. A modern remake of the film could explore what happens when evidence can be faked, edited, or dismissed as a deepfake in seconds. Jack’s obsession with proving what he heard would hit even harder in a world where nobody knows what to believe anymore. The original’s devastating ending is also a big part of why audiences rejected it back then, but it works perfectly today. Blow Out is a near-perfect film, but its central idea is begging to be updated for the age of misinformation.

Marathon Man is the movie that made an entire generation afraid of going to the dentist. The story follows history graduate Babe Levy (Dustin Hoffman), who spends his free time training for a marathon. His life is turned upside down when his older brother, Doc (Roy Scheider), turns out to be a secret government agent who has gotten tangled up with Dr. Christian Szell (Laurence Olivier), a Nazi war criminal hiding in South America. What’s worse is that Szell has come to New York to collect a fortune in stolen diamonds, and he is convinced that Babe knows something that could put them at risk. Marathon Man, written by William Goldman from his own novel, is famous for the scene where Szell tortures Babe with dental tools, along with the one where Holocaust survivors recognize him on the streets of New York’s diamond district.

Olivier’s menacing performance earned him an Oscar nomination for the role and practically defined the film. Hoffman also deserves his flowers for portraying Babe’s confusion with extreme conviction, which made the audience sympathize with him every step of the way. Nearly 50 years later, the idea of a war criminal hiding in plain sight, protected by money and powerful friends, still feels frighteningly relevant. Most younger viewers have never seen the original, though, and a fresh version could introduce them to one of the most unsettling stories the genre has ever produced.

The Parallax View is the ultimate paranoid thriller, and it might be even more unsettling today than it was in the 1970s. The film begins with the assassination of a U.S. senator at the top of Seattle’s Space Needle. Years later, reporter Joe Frady (Warren Beatty) notices that witnesses to the killing keep dying one after another. His investigation leads him to the Parallax Corporation, a shadowy company that seems to be recruiting troubled men and training them to become assassins.

The film, directed by Alan J. Pakula, who also made All the President’s Men, was released at a time when Americans had lost faith in the people in charge after a string of political assassinations and the Watergate scandal. Its most famous scene is a disturbing montage that Parallax uses to test its recruits, where people are shown flashing images of family and patriotism alongside violence until it’s hard to tell the difference. That idea of a company quietly searching for angry, lonely men to manipulate feels eerily close to how online radicalization works today. A remake could easily swap the old-fashioned test for social media algorithms, and it would be just as terrifying. Paramount+ announced plans for a series version back in 2021, but there has been little news since, and The Parallax View is long overdue for an update.

Wait Until Dark features one of the scariest showdowns in movie history, and it’s the perfect candidate for a remake. The film, based on Frederick Knott’s play, stars Audrey Hepburn as Susy Hendrix, a woman who recently lost her sight and lives in a New York City apartment with her husband, Sam (Efrem Zimbalist Jr.). Without realizing it, Sam brings home a doll that has been stuffed with heroin, and a group of criminals led by the ruthless Roat (Alan Arkin) will do anything to get it back. They come up with an elaborate con to trick Susy into handing it over, but it turns out she is not one to underestimate.

The film’s climax is what most people remember it for. Susy realizes that if she can’t see, the best way to win is to make sure nobody else can either, and she smashes every light in the apartment. When the film first came out, some theaters even dimmed their lights to make the sequence feel even scarier. The problem is that much of the first half has aged poorly, since almost everyone around Susy treats her like a helpless child. A remake could keep the brilliant premise while giving Susy the strength and intelligence she deserves from the very first scene. Hepburn earned an Oscar nomination for the role, but Wait Until Dark is ready for a brand-new heroine who can outsmart her attackers right from the start.

The Bose SoundLink Flex SE is a portable Bluetooth speaker with an IP67 waterproof rating. The speaker even floats in the water, so you can bring it with you into the pool. It also features a speakerphone, allowing you to take calls and speak with it. It's light and portable, and the Bluetooth 5.3 supports multipoint connectivity and SBC, AAC, and aptX codecs. It holds 12 hours of battery life (up to 20 hours with certain settings), has an IPX5 water resistance rating, and has LED lights that sync to the music. You can get it for $99 (originally $199).

This laptop comes with an Intel Ultra 5 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 16GB of RAM (which, honestly, is the minimum anyone should be buying in 2026).

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

#3407. The Masterpiece Heist Thriller That Inspired Michael B. Jordan’s New Film Officially Hits Free Streaming

Conor Sheeran is a Movies and TV features writer for Collider. He has a deep passion for cinema and watches everything from the biggest blockbusters to the smallest indies. While he specializes in movies and television, he has also written about politics, culture, and sports throughout his career. Based in New York City, Conor is also a massive fan of the New York Jets, Mets, and Knicks. He is still waiting for any of those teams to bring home a championship in his lifetime. A member of the National Writers Union and the International Federation of Journalists, Conor is a strong proponent of press freedom and collective action.

Heist films are one of cinema's most timeless genres. Whether set in modern times, the 1960s, or the deep past, a good movie about people willing to break the law in exciting ways remains one of the most reliable forms of filmmaking. As Michael B. Jordan prepares to introduce audiences to a new and updated version of a Hollywood classic, the original film that served as its inspiration is now available to stream for free.

Premiering in 1968, The Thomas Crown Affair stars Steve McQueen and Faye Dunaway in one of the best heist movies ever made, and one that remains endlessly cool decades after release. The movie inspired another remake in 1999, starring Pierce Brosnan and Rene Russo, which swapped the original's bank robbery for a more elaborate art theft, something that Jordan's upcoming remake seems to be incorporating. With Jordan's upcoming adaptation starring himself alongside Adria Arjona set to release early in 2027, there's no better time to revisit the original classic. Fortunately for audiences, it is now available to stream for free on platforms including Tubi, Pluto TV, and Roku.

The central plot of The Thomas Crown Affair centers on Thomas Crown (McQueen), a wealthy businessman who appears to have everything anyone could want: He's handsome, successful, and enjoys a luxury lifestyle that many can only dream of. Despite his success, Crown finds himself incredibly bored with his comfortable existence. This boredom manifests itself in a rather interesting way: he orchestrates an elaborate bank robbery, despite having no need for the money. Unlike traditional crime thrillers that tend to follow criminals who are down on their luck or desperate for money, The Thomas Crown Affair introduces a criminal who is motivated entirely by the thrill of getting away with something extraordinary.

Crown's confidence is soon challenged by an investigator, Vicki Anderson (Dunaway), who begins looking into the robbery to discover who could be behind the audacious crime. What follows is a cat-and-mouse game between Crown and Anderson, leading both to realize the romantic attraction that builds as each learns more about the other. It's a fascinating psychological battle between two intelligent adversaries, a duel that is only more exciting to watch thanks to the performances of McQueen and Dunaway. McQueen's effortlessly charismatic performance exudes cool, and it's easy to see how someone could be swayed by his charm, while Dunaway is the perfect foil. She knows what it would take to stop a man like Crown, but she also struggles to resist the temptation to be with him.

The enduring appeal of a story like The Thomas Crown Affair extends far beyond just McQueen and Dunaway's performances. Norman Jewison's direction gives the film a sleek, immersive style through its split-screen photography and editing, creating a distinctive look. The styling, costumes, on-set location shoots, and incredible score set the stage for an unforgettable experience. The Thomas Crown Affair helped establish a format for films like Ocean's Eleven and Entrapment that followed later, so it's easy to see how timeless this movie is and why a modern remake makes sense.

Michael B. Jordan's remake will take inspiration from the original and the 1999 version with Pierce Brosnan and Rene Russo, swapping a bank robbery for art thefts. This will mark Jordan's second time in the director's chair following Creed III; he will also produce and star alongside Adria Arjona, Kenneth Branagh, and Lily Gladstone. While many heist movies emphasize action, often using it as the anchor for the project, The Thomas Crown Affair demonstrates that compelling characters with psychological tension can be just as entertaining. The greatest strength of both films was the romantic and sexual tension between their leads, and, judging by the trailers, Jordan seems to be following in their footsteps.

Jordan's interpretation will certainly bring its own unique perspective to the source material, but the original film with McQueen and Dunaway remains a must-watch and the gold standard. For those eager to sink their teeth into a good heist movie and see the one that started it all, it's available to stream and, best of all, it's free on Tubi, Pluto TV, and Roku. Needless to say, McQueen's crime thriller is still essential viewing even nearly 60 years later.

#3406. iPhone 18, iPhone Air 2 get new release timing updates

Apple only launched high-end ‘Pro’ and ‘Duo’ iPhones this fall, marking a departure from previous years when more affordable models debuted too. But iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 are still coming, and a new report offers an update on release timing.

A new report from Kim Yeong-ho at ETNews provides a fresh update on timing for the iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2.

Rumors have indicated for well over a year that Apple planned to push these models out of the typical fall launch window and introduce them in early 2027 instead.

Per ETNews, Samsung and LG are providing the display panels for the new models, with Samsung the sole supplier for iPhone Air 2 and both companies splitting orders for iPhone 18. And their mass production plans signal a March release for the products.

Samsung Display plans to begin mass production in January, while LG Display will start late this year…The Korean panel makers appear to be aligning their production plans with an expected March launch.

A March launch window lines up well with when Apple tends to ramp up product introductions following a slower winter. Earlier this year, iPhone 17e debuted in March alongside new Macs and the iPad Air.

The year before, however, the iPhone 16e arrived in February instead.

With Apple shaking up its normal iPhone rollout schedule, it was anyone’s guess how soon the new models would debut. But a March launch makes sense and gives Apple a trio of new iPhones every six months—three unveiled in September, and another three in March.

Are you holding out for an iPhone 18 or iPhone Air 2? Let us know in the comments.

#3403. Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow review: Heavenly comfort for hot sleepers

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow is one of the most comfortable pillows I’ve tested for Tom's Guide, and more than lives up to its luxury $135 price tag. A shredded memory foam and latex fill hugs your head while supporting your neck no matter the position you sleep in. The shredded foam and cotton cover also keeps the pillow breathable and cool even on warm nights. However, while the Saatva Cloud delivered supreme comfort, heavy and tall side sleepers who need firmer support should look elsewhere.

Lacks firm support for tall and heavy bodies

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Saatva is the luxury sleep brand behind the number one rated option in our best mattress of the year guide, the Saatva Classic (see our Saatva Classic mattress review), which is why I'm always eager to test the Saatva's sleep accessories that deliver the brand's signature luxury for less. Along with its mattress toppers and bed sheets, Saatva also offers a line-up of premium pillows, one of which is the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow.

Filled with shredded gel-infused memory foam, the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow promises universal support and comfort — so I tested it for a week to see if it's worthy of a place in our best pillow guide.

Despite the name, the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow isn't made completely out of memory foam; it also contains natural latex. And after testing it for a week, I'm happy to say that if I’m going to sleep on a memory foam pillow, I want to sleep on this one.

Type: Memory foam and natural latexBest for: Combination sleepers and hot sleepersSizes: queen and king, standard and high loftTrial: 45 nightsWarranty: 1 yearPrice: $135 at Saatva

The Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow is sold in a standard and high loft with a breathable cotton cover that’s removable and washable. Inside the cover is a mixture of memory foam and natural latex pieces that create a comfortable and huggable pillow. The shredded foam design worked well with the cotton cover to prevent any overheating at night.

I tested the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow in a standard loft and, though I sunk slightly into it, the pillow seemed to settle to the perfect height needed to sleep comfortably on my back and stomach.

While I could sleep on my side on the standard loft, I would suggest the high loft for side sleepers who need more support. This pillow gave me no reason to doubt its durability as it always returned to its shape when I got up in the morning.

A starting price of $135 does push the Cloud Memory Foam Pillow into the premium price tier, but it's not completely surprising for a luxury sleep brand like Saatva. However, you can sometimes catch a bundle deal that can save you up to $60 when you buy two.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow is breathable and comfortable for all sleep types. Starting at $135, it’s a luxury buy, although for Black Friday you can save when you buy a pair of pillows. Buyers also receive a 45-night trial and one-year warranty when they order this pillow.

A standard queen size Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow is $135, which puts it into a premium category. Saatva rarely, if ever, includes pillows in the monthly Saatva mattress sales, but it sometimes has cut-price deals on a pair of pillows during sales events such as the Black Friday mattress sales.

In fact, the current Saatva Black Friday mattress sales have a deal where you can save up to $60 when you buy two Cloud Memory Foam Pillows at Saatva.

If this pillow was filled solely with memory foam, I’d say it was overpriced. The natural latex added to the fill and a cotton cover make the price feel more reasonable, though I think a removable fill to make the height adjustable at home would make this pillow feel like better value.

Saatva offers a 45-night trial and a one-year warranty with the purchase of this pillow. Brands like Bearaby only offer 30-day trials, so an extra 15 days is nice, until you consider the generous trial offered with the Coop Adjustable Latex Pillow — 100 nights and 5 years warranty for some of its latex pillows.

The Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow can be ordered in two sizes – queen and king – and two loft heights — standard and high. The standard loft is 4"-5" tall, while the high loft is 6"-7" in height.

This pillow has a breathable organic cotton knit cover (though it doesn’t have organic certifications) that’s removable and washable.

Despite the name of the pillow, the fill is comprised of both shredded gel-infused CertiPUR-US memory foam and natural latex foam. According to Saatva, the Cloud Memory Foam Pillow is hypoallergenic.

I slept on the Helix Cooling Memory Foam Pillow for a week and performed a series of objective and subjective tests, following our pillow testing methodology.

The Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow arrived in a clear plastic bag within a cardboard box. It wasn’t vacuum sealed, meaning when I pulled it out of the plastic bag, it was ready to be slept on.

There weren’t any noticeable off-gassing smells when I pulled it from the packaging, but to be fair, I was really congested during the testing period because of hay fever.

However, when I slept on the pillow, there was an almond smell to it, which is a fairly common off-gassing scent for memory foam products.

The previous Saatva pillow I tested was too tall and didn’t have much give — which is why I breathed a sigh of relief the first time I laid my head on the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow.

I tested a queen standard loft and discovered it to be the perfect size for someone like me who likes to sleep on her stomach, back, and side.

The shredded fill of this pillow spreads when weight is placed on it, but not enough that my head sunk down to the bed.

As I moved my head on the pillow, the pillow felt malleable and soft, hugging my head in a comforting way. I particularly like how this pillow feels when I’m lying on my back and stomach, as my head sinks enough to align my spine, lulling me to sleep quickly.

I can sleep on my side with the standard loft size. However, I think the high loft would be better if I was strictly a side sleeper.

When the pillow eventually breaks down, I can see myself sleeping on my side less and less with this pillow and reverting to my back or stomach. Those with broad shoulders should choose the high loft size from the get-go.

I placed a 15lb weight in the center of the pillow, and it sunk over an inch. That makes sense considering the foams inside are shredded. When I lifted the dumbbell, the pillow sprung back into shape immediately, which is a good sign of the its durability.

I didn’t wake up hot or sweaty when sleeping on the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow, and that’s all thanks to Saatva’s temperature regulation. Memory foam is a far more heat-retaining material than natural latex, so to mitigate any overheating issues, Saatva utilized organic cotton for the cover — which is breathable — and shredded the memory foam and latex interior fill so air could weave its way through and keep my temperature neutral at night.

During the beginning of testing, I was sleeping without the air-conditioner and just a fan, so it was about 75 degrees in my house when I fell asleep at night and around 70 degrees when I woke up in the morning. The fact that heat did not build up during that time was very promising, and most likely what you can expect throughout the year.

A good rule of thumb: replace your pillows every two years and keep an eye on how quickly your pillow bounces back over time.

This can be done by folding your pillow in half. A slow bounce back means the fill has worn down. Until the pillow breaks down, maintenance will ensure it lasts longer.

After a week of testing, I haven’t noticed any sagging or break down of the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow. The shredded nature of the memory foam and latex fill means you may not be laying your head on the same bits of foam each night, which will probably result in a longer lifespan.

The cotton cover also appears durable, and if well maintained (i.e. washed) it should hold up for at least two years. If it does break down, you could easily replace the cover, but I don’t see that happening.

Thankfully, Saatva offers a one-year limited warranty on this pillow so if you notice anything out of the ordinary, take advantage of the warranty.

It wasn’t until I was an adult that I realized how important it is to take care of your pillow. They easily absorb sweat, night creams, and all manner of stuff from your head and face. Maintenance ensures they last longer.

The Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow is made of two parts — the cover and the fill. The cover can be removed and machine washed on cold on a delicate cycle, and either hung to dry or tumbled dry on low.

You can’t throw the memory foam and latex fill into the wash, but you can spot clean it if you need to.

Comfort is the most important thing to me when it comes to a pillow and the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow delivered.

The cloud-like and huggable surface is conducive to a good night’s sleep, especially since it’s supportive enough to keep your head and spine aligned no matter what position you sleep in. If you prefer to sleep on your side, I would order the high loft option, as it’ll offer more support for a longer period of time.

The cotton cover and the shredded natural latex and memory foam fill results in a breathable design, so you won’t sleep hot or sweat at night.

During the testing period, the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow bounced back quickly, leading us to believe that it’ll last the full two years of a pillow's lifetime. Especially if you wash the cover consistently.

All in all, this supportive and huggable pillow will cradle your head and lead to a comfortable night’s sleep.

✅ You overheat at night: This pillow is breathable, thanks to a cotton cover and an interior fill of shredded latex and memory foam.

✅ You're a combi sleeper: This pillow has the right amount of give and support for those who like to sleep on their stomach, back, and side. I suggest the high loft option for side sleepers.

✅ You like to try your pillow for a decent amount of time: Saatva lets buyers test a pillow for 45 days. If you don’t like it, Saatva will accept a return and give you a full refund.

❌ You prefer organic materials: This pillow does have some memory foam and while it’s CertiPUR-US certified, that doesn’t mean its free of toxins or VOCs, only that it’s low enough to be considered “safe.” Neither the natural latex, nor the organic cotton used in the fill and the cover are certified as organic despite claims by Saatva.

❌ You like to customize the size of your pillow: While you can order this pillow in high or low loft, unfortunately, Saatva didn’t design it so you could remove or add fill and thus adjust the height in your own home.

❌ You like a supportive, firm feel: Your head is going to sink into this soft and cloud-like pillow. For a more supportive and firm feel, try Saatva’s Down Alternative Pillow.

The Helix Talalay Latex pillow is a good alternative for those who don’t like their head sinking too far into their pillow as it’s made from a single piece of foam. Expect a bouncier feel. Made with Talalay latex and perforated with holes, this pillow will help you stay cool all night long. It comes in two loft options and you can get this pillow for as little as $111, which is more affordable than the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow.

As the name of this pillow indicates, the Coop Sleep Good Adjustable Latex Pillow is adjustable. It's made with a blend of natural Talalay latex and microfibers, and comes with an extra bag of fill so you can add more if necessary and create the loft and feel you prefer. Our reviewer reports that the pillow is breathable and prevents heat from trapping. A 100-night trial and a 5-year warranty is worth having, too.

If you want buttery soft comfort for a budget price, then I reccomend the viral Squishmallows SquishPillow, which is just $29.99 in a standard size. Currently our No 1 budget pick thanks to our glowing SquishPillow review (which praised its plush comfort and reliable support), the SquishPillow comes in a medium, firm or soft.

#3402. iPhone Duo is getting three new features in iOS 27.3

iOS 27.3 launches next month and includes several exciting changes for iPhone Duo, here’s what’s new for Apple’s foldable model.

Apple is granting iPhone Duo users one of their biggest feature requests: face unlock is coming with iOS 27.3.

Face unlock isn’t a full-fledged Face ID, and it doesn’t work for features like Apple Pay, but it is a convenient new option for unlocking your iPhone Duo just by looking at it. Per Apple:

Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

If your iPhone Duo has gone unused for 45 minutes or more, face unlock won’t work and you’ll need to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. But for most users, that probably just means using Touch ID first thing in the morning, then relying on face unlock the rest of the day.

On a related note, you can also enable Attention Aware features in iOS 27.3. These are available whether you use the face unlock feature or not, but are limited to the outer display. Once enabled, they can automatically lower the volume of alarms and timers, keep the display from dimming, and more.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo

Reachability is available on other iPhone models to move onscreen content down vertically, closer to your thumb. But on iPhone Duo with iOS 27.3, Apple has a unique twist on the feature.

Instead of helping you reach content vertically, Reachability on iPhone Duo works horizontally.

If you’re using the outer screen and find that buttons or other UI elements are out of reach, you can swipe from the side to have onscreen content shift closer to your thumb.

You can always disable Reachability if you find yourself accidentally triggering it too often. But if one-handed iPhone Duo use gives you trouble, Reachability is a great new option to have.

Read more: iOS 27.3 introduces new iPhone Duo feature for one-handed use

What should happen when you close your iPhone Duo’s folding screen? Apple has found that users have different preferences. Some want the iPhone to stay unlocked for continued use, while others prefer that it automatically locks when closed.

In iOS 27.3, Apple adds a new setting so users can enable whichever behavior they prefer.

By default, iPhone Duo will work as it always has, staying unlocked after being closed. But inside Settings ⇾ Display & Brightness, iOS 27.3 provides the option of automatically locking upon being closed instead. You could achieve something similar before with Shortcuts, but now there’s a built-in setting too.

It’s not exactly a “new feature,” but iPhone Duo users will also find that the system keyboard has changed in iOS 27.3. Apple tweaked the outer display keyboard to push keys closer together and make one-handed use easier.

Here’s a comparison of the old and new keyboards via Beta Profiles on X:

iOS 27.3 beta tweaks iPhone Duo's outer display keyboard, with narrower keys and a slightly thinner, smaller font. pic.twitter.com/BDKCBZc52Z

Read more: iOS 27.3 changes the iPhone Duo keyboard, here’s how

Which new iPhone Duo features in iOS 27.3 are you most excited for? Let us know in the comments.

#3401. Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

You know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”

At this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

To borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

The problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

For example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

Those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT showed me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

While most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”

The reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

This pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic."

If there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

One of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

In every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

The generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

This is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

To a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

That means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

#3397. The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: Looksmaxxing With Dangerous Drugs

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.)

In the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart quickly led to women posting the waist heart.

Okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

As if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber shows up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?"

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood."

Nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

#3393. iOS 27.3 adds Siri AI usage limits, here’s what counts toward your limit

Earlier this week, Apple revealed that Siri AI usage limits will be implemented in iOS 27.3 and explained how iCloud+ increases those limits. Now we have a real-world example of what it looks like when limits are hit, and details on what counts toward those limits.

Siri AI and select other AI features will begin having usage limits in iOS 27.3 for advanced tasks.

This is standard practice with other AI services like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude because these tools rely on server-based models rather than running entirely on-device.

Here’s an example from the iOS 27.3 beta showing what it looks like when you hit your Siri AI daily usage limit. Per Ben in a post on X:

I hit my Siri AI usage limit, it still works though, including complex questions pic.twitter.com/XYYNPMnSnn

In a follow-up post, Ben clarifies that complex questions did stop working shortly after posting. As expected though, basic requests continued to work as usual—they don’t have a usage limit.

One question that Apple hasn’t made clear is what qualifies as a complex or “advanced” Siri AI request. The company shares just two examples of something advanced:

Suppose it gets it wrong like it does most of the time. I wonder if that still counts.

But leaker pdfu has discovered exactly the instructions Siri AI follows to determine whether a request counts as basic or advanced. In a post on X he outlines the parameters for requests deemed “advanced.”

Siri AI will check the request against this list, and if it involves any of these, it’s deemed “advanced.”

It would be helpful if Apple publicly documented these guidelines for users. But perhaps after iOS 27.3 ships and usage limits are fully implemented, we’ll get more detail from the company.

What do you think of Siri AI’s parameters for advanced requests in iOS 27.3? Let us know in the comments.

There’s such a gratifying feeling that comes from finishing a really good book, closing it up, reflecting on its quality and placing it back on your bookshelf.

I spend a good deal of time flipping through autobiographies written by my favorite wrestlers, musicians and media personalities. Visual history books dedicated to the video games, comic books and anime I love also keep me entertained for hours. I’m always searching for the next great book that’ll keep me from staring at my phone and reading rage-baiting tweets in my spare time.

ChatGPT is capable of stepping up to be everyone's personal book curator. It has certainly put me on the right path to finding even more quality reads based on what it knows about the genres I like, the authors I’m a fan of and even the sort of books that I’m not really all that into.

These prompts have helped expand my collection of books, and I’m sure they’ll do the same for all my fellow bookworms reading this right now. Try any of these out and see where ChatGPT leads you next on your journey for more quality literature.

Inputting any of the following seven prompts into ChatGPT, while also providing it with your literary tastes, favorite authors, preferred styles of writing that compel you the most and current mood, will help it highlight a list of books you may end up adoring next.

The first prompt works quite well in commanding ChatGPT to examine the deeper literary qualities attached to your favorite books. The second prompt works to showcase the type of books that deliver the same type of emotional experiences you derived from your last read. The third prompt is perfect for book hunters who are on the lookout for less celebrated books that you may not have known about beforehand. The fourth prompt is the ultimate mood-book matcher, as it takes note of how you’re currently feeling and shows you the type of books that could get you out of a mental funk or put you in a more relaxing mood.

The fifth prompt puts ChatGPT in the mindset of a book recommendation engine that gives you the sort of books that explore genres you may have overlooked. The sixth prompt goes even further to help ChatGPT suggest what books you should read, as it mentions both your literary likes and dislikes.

As for the seventh and final prompt, it works as a survey that gives ChatGPT everything it could possibly know about you to give you the best book recommendations possible.

Feel free to refer to the seven prompts listed below and try them out for yourself to see where your next book-filled adventures lead you next:

And as an extra follow-up response, this next prompt can help ChatGPT do another round of evaluation to see which books truly match your tastes and weed out any made-up books it may have suggested:

Now challenge your own recommendations. Which [number] books on this list are the weakest matches for my tastes, and why? Replace them with better alternatives. Don't invent titles or authors, and tell me where you're uncertain.

Running to ChatGPT to tell it to recommend you a bunch of new and old books worth reading without being as descriptive as possible about your tastes is a waste of time. The chatbot needs every piece of information about your interests across the literary spectrum to tailor its book recommendations to match everything you enjoy (and don’t enjoy as much).

Hopefully, by the end of each ChatGPT session that kicks off with any of these prompts, you’ll leave it with one or a bunch of strong suggestions that could keep you and your book club occupied for months on end. Let me know how you get on in the comments below.

ChatGPT dictation is getting a boost today. OpenAI has updated the speech-to-text feature with Live Dictation that improves both speed and reliability. The enhanced dictation update also removes the 10-minute limit.

“Dictation in ChatGPT is getting faster and more reliable,” OpenAI announced on X.

“With Live Dictation, your speech turns into text as you talk, so you spend less time waiting for your message to finish transcribing,” the company continued.

Atty Eleti, who works on voice features at OpenAI, added that the 10-minute dictation limit has also been removed as part of the dictation streaming upgrade.

Dictation in ChatGPT is getting faster and more reliable.

With Live Dictation, your speech turns into text as you talk, so you spend less time waiting for your message to finish transcribing. Tap or click on the waveform to show or hide text as you go. We’ve also removed the 10-minute recording limit.

Live Dictation is rolling out globally to all ChatGPT plans on iOS, Android, web, and the desktop app.

#3382. The Sony PlayStation Pulse costs just $99 but delivers life-like and detailed sound that punches way above its weight — and it’s a must-have for PS5 players

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Suave looks, premium build, comfortable plush ear cushions, and drool-worthy sound — these make the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset one of the best PS5 headsets around. Fitted with custom planar drivers designed in collaboration with Audeze, the Pulse delivers life-like sound across genres. 30 hours of battery life and simultaneous dual-point connectivity are cherries on top of the cake. However, I wish the bass was more powerful and the headset had a mobile companion app.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset improves on its predecessors in nearly every way to deliver one of the best gaming headsets of 2026. Sony’s Tempest 3D Audio works in conjunction with the headset’s planar drivers, creating excellent life-like, rich and directional sound. The Pulse is mighty comfortable and looks great. It offers up to 30 hours of battery life, and its mic performance is much better than its pricier sibling.

But it pains me to say that this headset isn’t perfect. While customization is easy through your PS5’s settings, I wish there was a mobile companion app for those using the headset with their computers or phones. And while the overall sound quality is amazing, the bass sounds a little thin.

Should you still buy it? I think so. To find out why, read my full Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset review.

PlayStation 5, PlayStation Portal, PC, macOS, Android, iOS

From its suave looks and respectable battery life, to its detailed sound and affordable price point, the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset is an excellent headset for PS5 gamers.

As someone who’s been loyal to PlayStation for a decade, I’ve always loved the consoles’ sleek and premium design. While the original Sony PlayStation Pulse 3D Wireless Headset ($99) wasn’t bad-looking per se, I much prefer the minimalist approach Sony has taken towards the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset.

The new headset sports an understated design with round earcups that is still, at its core, quintessentially Sony. Available in either Midnight Black or White, I think the Pulse looks brilliant. It doesn’t draw attention to itself, and its simple design means you can use it as a regular set of cans when you’re traveling.

In addition to its good looks, the Pulse is mighty comfortable, too. The faux leather ear cushions are soft with a matte texture, and the earcups are spacious enough that they engulf my ears perfectly. Even after seven straight hours of wear, my ears didn’t feel sweaty or too hot. The pads can be twisted off, too, in case they get damaged and need replacing.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

On the Pulse’s headband, you’ll find foam cushioning that helps alleviate pressure you’d otherwise feel on the top of your head. However, this cushioning feels like it’s made up of more air than anything else. I don’t necessarily think this is a massive drawback as the Pulse is a fairly lightweight headset.

The Pulse weighs just 10.58 ounces. That’s similar to the Pulse 3D (10.37 ounces) but lighter than the first-party Pulse Elite ($149, 12.2 ounces) and third-party Cherry XTRFY H3 ($99, 11.46 ounces). Sony hasn’t compromised on the Pulse’s build quality while maintaining its light frame either, as the headset feels solid.

As has become tradition for Sony at this point, it has fitted with PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset with custom planar magnetic drivers (four magnets per driver). These have been developed in collaboration with Audeze, the audio giant of Maxwell 2 ($329) fame, and a brand Sony acquired back in 2023. The drivers are programmed to deliver three-dimensional life-like sound across genres — and the Pulse excels at doing just that.

To take full advantage of the sound quality, I recommend diving into your PS5’s settings and creating your personalized 3D sound profile (it takes around five minutes). PlayStation’s Tempest 3D Audio, in conjunction with the Pulse’s planar drivers, delivers phenomenal spatial and directional audio. I tested it out by playing Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced, and Cyberpunk 2077 on my PS5 Slim.

In AC Black Flag Resynced, I appreciated how immersed the 3D Audio made me feel. At this price, the directional audio is phenomenal. I could tell exactly which direction the sounds were coming from. When surrounded by small and big ships during naval combat, I could pinpoint their locations even when I couldn’t see them. My ship’s creaking was loud and clear, adding to the immersion. When on land, I loved hearing rain falling on the palm trees right overhead, like they were actually falling above me.

Directional audio proved effective in Cyberpunk 2077, too, where I used it to my advantage to listen out for footsteps and determine my enemies’ positions. This made stealthily infiltrating enemy camps a walk in the park. The Pulse also has a wide soundstage with every aspect sounding well-balanced. Bullets sounded sharp as they whizzed past and ricocheted off the walls.

Dialogues across all three games sounded detailed and life-like, especially in Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 which has some of the best voice acting known to man (argue with the wall). I could feel the emotions in the characters’ voices, and the wobble in their throats was clear during certain scenes. The Pulse made cutscenes feel dramatic and immersive. My only complaint with the Pulse is the bass… which I’ll discuss in detail shortly.

Does the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset have the longest battery life in its price range? Nope, the Cherry XTRFY H3 with its 100-hour rating takes the crown, but the Pulse doesn’t give you much to complain about. Sony says that the headset should last you up to 30 hours between charges — that’s 18 hours longer than the Pulse 3D (12-hour rating) and the same as the pricier Pulse Elite.

Given that I have a full-time job, I couldn’t play games for 30 hours to test the Pulse’s battery life (I wish I could…), so instead, I left it running overnight with Cyberpunk 2077 running at 50% volume on my PS5. I was prompted to charge the headset around the 29-hour mark. Your mileage will naturally depend on volume and other settings, but good to see that Sony’s rating is fairly accurate.

When we reviewed the OG Sony PlayStation Pulse 3D, we found its microphone to be underwhelming. Similarly, the Sony PlayStation Pulse Elite’s mic was simply okay and nothing special. That’s why I am so pleased that the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset’s mic is much, much improved.

The Pulse features a built-in integrated mic with AI-powered noise rejection, and it makes you sound loud and clear. I tested the mic by calling my friend, Harry, who was also testing the headset for TechRadar (our sister site). I was pleasantly surprised by how warm he sounded — and he said the same about my voice. There was plenty of nuance in his voice and his words didn’t bleed into one another. When I was hovering over the Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 icon, his voice still came through clearly without being overpowered by the background music.

Even though it doesn’t feature a detachable boom mic, the Pulse’s mic’s performance feels on par with that of the Cherry XTRFY H3, and it even upstages the Turtle Beach Stealth 500 ($99).

The Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset is compatible with the PlayStation 5, PlayStation Portal, Windows and macOS machines, and iOS and Android smartphones. There are two ways of connecting the Pulse to your device. Simply plug in the included PlayStation Link USB-C dongle into your console or laptop for lag-free audio, and you’re good to go. There’s also Bluetooth connectivity for connecting to the Portal (which has PlayStation Link built into it).

What’s even better is that the Pulse features audio mixing and dual-point connectivity. What this basically means is that if you’ve got the Pulse connected to your phone via Bluetooth and to your PS5 using the dongle, you’ll be able to listen to both at the same time. No need to swap sources manually or pause one to listen to the other. Want to watch/listen to a YouTube tutorial while playing GTA 6? Easily done.

Audio mixing isn’t a brand new feature as we’ve seen it on headsets like the Razer Barracuda V2 Pro ($199)... but it’s also missing from headsets that cost more than the Pulse, like the Logitech G Pro X3 Lightspeed ($249) and the Fractal Design Scape ($199). That’s a win for Sony in my book.

One of the best things about the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset is that it doesn’t break the bank. It has a retail price of $99 at Amazon U.S. / £89 at Currys U.K. and given the trend with other Pulse models, I expect the Pulse to receive major price cuts during sales events next year.

The Pulse is priced similarly to the OG Pulse 3D ($99), the Cherry XTRFY H3 ($99), and it’s cheaper than the Pulse Elite ($149). I also think it offers more bang for your buck compared to the latter. The Pulse is also $100 cheaper than the Pulse Explore earbuds ($199). If you’re willing to wait until early 2027, the Pulse Edge will be launching with even more features, but naturally, I expect it to be pricier than the Pulse.

There isn’t a lot wrong with the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset, but it’s important to note that there’s no smartphone app, and the bass sounds slightly thin.

While I love the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset’s wide soundstage and life-like sound (as I waxed lyrical about earlier), I really wish the bass was more powerful. In Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, I found that my magic attacks didn’t land with much oomph. Luna’s Elemental Trick and Elemental Genesis are meant to rumble and shake the ground, but that wasn’t the case through the Pulse.

Similarly, in Control, the Hiss’ low-end drone felt more like a buzz, which meant that the alien-like enemies didn’t feel as unnerving as they do through a high-end headset, like the Razer BlackShark V3 Pro ($249). You’ll need to spend a lot more to get full-bodied sound.

As I mentioned earlier, the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset’s settings can be adjusted via the PS5’s settings — and there’s no other way to do it. Yes, even though the headset is compatible with computers and smartphones, you won’t be able to change its equalizer and other settings unless you have access to a PS5.

I wouldn’t say this is a dealbreaker per se as the Pulse is a PlayStation-first headset. But I would caution against getting it if you play across multiple platforms. A headset like the Logitech G325 Lightspeed ($79) or the Turtle Beach Stealth 500 might be better suited to your needs if that’s the case.

The Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset might not be perfect but it’s still a darn good set of cans. Sporting plush ear cushions that feel like hugs for your ears, the Pulse is supremely comfortable for long gaming sessions. 30 hours of battery life, dual-point connectivity, and strong mic performance are great, but it's the headset’s 3D audio that will quickly win you over.

While its soundstage is commendable, the Pulse struggles to reproduce ground-shaking bass (which is to be expected at this price). Customizing the headset is easy through your PS5’s settings but if you plan on using it with your smartphone or computer, you won’t find any companion apps on those platforms.

At the end of the day, if you’re after detailed, life-like sound that feels immersive, and a comfortable fit that doesn’t hurt your ears after a few hours, I can’t recommend the Pulse enough. It punches way above its weight.
