#3380. There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication issues." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen."

But to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering new security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find new security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be said for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

You might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October update. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

It's important to understand that just about every company that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as quickly as possible.

The implications aren't specific to any one company, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

#3378. Apple among the companies facing pressure from US senators over ‘nudify’ apps [U: Apple, TTP respond]

The Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps. Here are the details.

Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable users to generate nonconsensual nude images.

According to the updated rules, apps that allow users to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.

Apple also warns that apps used primarily for pornographic content or the objectification of real people may be removed from the App Store without notice.

While definitely well-intended, Apple’s changes came amid growing reports of AI-powered nudify apps, which easily allow users to generate nonconsensual intimate images.

Two months before these changes, Apple removed an app that allowed users to create pornographic deepfakes of real people after WIRED reached out for comment, which in turn came one month after San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu demanded that Apple and Google remove several nudify apps from their app stores.

Apple also removed several apps following investigations by the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), which published reports in January and April revealing that such apps were widely available on the App Store, sometimes even appearing in sponsored search results.

Throughout these investigations, Apple has maintained that nudify apps have always been prohibited under its App Review Guidelines, and that it proactively rejects and removes apps that violate its policies, including those flagged through user reports.

Apple, of course, is not alone in this challenge, with Google facing similar criticism over their availability on the Play Store, and Meta coming under scrutiny for allowing developers to advertise these apps on Facebook and Instagram, as highlighted in the WIRED report mentioned above.

Which brings us to today’s report from The Guardian.

According to The Guardian’s exclusive report, “three Senate Democrats sent letters to tech CEOs saying safeguards against nudification apps are insufficient on their platforms.”

A trio of US Senators say Apple and Google are failing to effectively detect and remove apps that can be used to generate nonconsensual nude or pornographic imagery. They also say Meta is continuing to profit off of ads for these so-called nudification apps that “victimize women and girls worldwide”.

The senators, namely Ron Wyden of Oregon, Ed Markey of Massachusetts, and Ben Luján of New Mexico, claim that in addition to failing to remove these apps, the companies may actually be profiting from their distribution and promotion.

Commenting on the letter, both Google and Meta said they prohibit such apps or their promotion and work to detect and remove violations from their platforms, broadly echoing what Apple has repeatedly stated when reached for comment in the past over these same issues.

However, Wyden’s office argues that simply reaffirming, or in Apple’s case, updating these policies, means little if the companies continue to struggle to enforce them.

Keith Chu, the chief communications adviser and deputy policy director to Wyden, said that clarifying policies is not the same thing as enforcing them. Despite the companies reaffirming the prohibition of these apps, they continue to proliferate across Apple and Google app stores or be promoted in ads on Meta platforms, he added.

In its latest investigation, published just last month, TTP found 135 apps capable of generating nude or pornographic imagery on the App Store and the Play Store, using accounts registered to 13-year-old boys.

Additionally, researchers found that even accounts configured with parental controls were able to download these apps without requiring parental approval.

Despite Apple and Google removing the apps identified in the investigation, The Guardian noted that these apps continued to work on devices where they had already been installed.

Now, Senator Wyden warns that Congress may need to step in if the companies fail to do a better job of cracking down on these apps.

To read The Guardian’s full report, follow this link.

Update, 8:40 p.m. ET: In a statement to 9to5Mac, Apple said:

“We designed the App Store to be a safe and trusted place for users. A number of the apps in the TTP report are mainstream photo and video editing tools with legitimate, widely used functionality, and do not have nudification or deepfake capabilities. We prohibit nudify apps on the App Store, and remove developers who add capabilities like it after the App Review process — a malicious tactic known as bait-and-switch. We previously removed 28 of the apps referenced in this report before it was shared with us and have taken action on the remaining apps found to violate our rules. The report also relies on testing from older software that does not reflect current Apple safety features, including expanded protections for teens and parental controls in Screen Time that give families the ability to block kids and teens from downloading apps rated above their age.”

Expanding on the safety features mentioned in its statement, Apple noted that teens aged 13 through 17 now have certain protections enabled by default, including web content filters, even if their parents haven’t configured any restrictions, and pointed to ⁠this support article for more information.

The company added that children under 13 are required to use Child Accounts, and that the report relied on its previous 17+ age rating system, which was replaced last year with a more granular system that includes 13+, 16+, and 18+ ratings.

Just curious. Why doesn't someone from Apple try out the app before approving it, rather than approving it and waiting until people complain? I know there are many thousands of apps on the App store. But given that Apple makes money off most of these apps, it could surely afford to hire a staff charged with reviewing submitted apps to ensure compliance with the App store's guidelines and requirements before making them available in the App store. What am I missing here?

Apple also noted that in its report, TTP counted apps depicting people in swimwear or lingerie, which the company said does not constitute nudification or, in itself, violate its guidelines.

As for parental controls, Apple explained that, although apps that exceed a child’s configured age restrictions won’t appear in curated App Store sections, they can still be found through search, allowing children to request permission to download them through Ask to Buy. Without parental approval, the download remains blocked.

Apple added that Ask to Buy is supposed to require parental approval even for purchases made using gift card balances, including subscriptions. The company said that if a purchase didn’t trigger an approval request, that would be unexpected behavior, and that it is investigating further.

Update, November 19, 4:00 p.m. ET: In response to Apple’s statement, TTP director Katie Paul reached out to 9to5Mac with the following comment:

Apple’s statement on nudify apps sidesteps important issues and leaves out key context. The company says it prohibits nudify apps but doesn’t address how its age rating system for apps contributes to the problem. TTP has shown how Apple relies on information provided by app developers to set age ratings—a self-reporting system that allows many nudify and pornographic apps to be misleadingly labeled a suitable for minors. Apple also continues to talk about removing nudify apps from the App Store, without mentioning that apps that are “removed” continue to be fully functional on people’s phones.

There are many questions about Apple’s policy on nudify apps that the statement fails to address. Apple has adopted a limited definition of “nudify.” The company defines nudify apps as capable of showing someone naked, not stripping them down to a bikini or lingerie. But the company also says it bans “creepy” and “nonconsensual intimate imagery.” What if an app is used to depict a woman in a bikini without her consent? We have asked Apple to clarify that and have not heard back.

As for Apple’s comment that TTP relied on “older software,” that may refer to the fact that Apple rolled out new child safety features in the fall. Our research was conducted in summer 2026. But many of Apple’s new features pertain to parent-supervised accounts on Apple, which have to be set up by a parent. Apple relies entirely on parents to go out of their way to locate and enable these settings. This raises obvious questions about how many people actually do this.

#3373. Zane Lowe shares Apple Music Radio audience numbers, recalls ‘crickets’ in the early days

In a new interview with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, Apple Music’s Zane Lowe discussed the early days of Apple Music Radio and revealed just how many people tune in each month. Here are the details.

Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.

In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue said Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.

Apple Music’s Zane Lowe, however, has now offered a more concrete figure, revealing that the service reaches over 50 million unique listeners every month:

We were never, you know, delusional enough to assume we were going to get a huge audience overnight. We’d have to build it like anyone else would have to build anything. But we’ve just got to a point in our 11 years on where we now, overall, reach over 50 million unique listeners a month, which is a really large number for us, and it’s growing exponentially and really fast.

The revelation came in a wide-ranging interview published today with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, where Lowe discussed Apple Music Radio’s early struggles, its approach to supporting emerging artists, and why human curation remains central to the service.

When discussing the early days at Apple Music, Lowe recalled:

When we started the radio here, I didn’t have access or opportunity with a lot of the artists that I built relationships with from the BBC because we were unproven. And I came over here thinking, “Well, I’ve got Jimmy Iovine over here, and I’ve got Apple over here and I feel unstoppable, and who’s not going to want to come and launch this thing with us?” But it was kind of crickets… As upsetting as that was at the time, two good things came out of it. Number one, it snapped me back into the reality force field of building something from scratch. And number two, it made us focus really clearly and in a big way on new and emerging artists.

He also mentioned some of the first artists Apple Music Radio supported, including Billie Eilish with “Ocean Eyes,” Khalid with American Teen, and Bryson Tiller with his first song.

At the time, Lowe noted, these artists were just getting started, and supporting emerging talent became a defining part of Apple Music Radio’s approach, one that continues to this day:

The really cool number is on our radio network. We played — this year alone — over 6,500 individual artists, which is not a commercial radio model. [Other radio networks’] playlists are very small, and the amount of plays is very great. Our playlist is gigantic. We play a lot of different artists, and over half of those 6,500 artists we’ve played in one year are new or emerging. So, think about 3,300 artists, roughly, getting played, who may be on their first song, their first EP, their first album…It’s proof of concept. It’s great.

Still on the subject of the early days at Apple Music, Lowe said “it was very clear [from the start] that that was very important to everybody who was responsible for bringing Apple Music to life,” adding that “serving artists and the artistic community in a way that is of most value and of most service” still drives “a lot of the decision-making” at the platform.

When the conversation turned to Apple Music’s recent rebranding, which introduced a new logo physically created using sound waves from a composition by Fred again.., Lowe said he couldn’t speak to the decisions behind it, but stressed the human element and the creative process that went into it:

We could have created that in a way that could utilize all of the tech available. We could type that into a prompt. But at the end of the day, seeing how it’s made is so much more additionally inspiring than just seeing it. It speaks to, I think, what we try to do here, which is, we love the process of what we do, and the result is a byproduct of getting to do it and loving to do it.

The issue of algorithms also came up when Lowe discussed Apple Music’s approach to music discovery, with the executive emphasizing the importance of human curation over automated recommendations:

Well, we don’t want to say that too loudly, because someone could be like, “Wait a minute, we could cut costs here? Man, how did we not think of that!” Look, I mean, jokes aside, we’ve been incredibly fortunate, and I’ve been incredibly fortunate to take that step from the BBC into a company and to work with people that value exactly what it is you’re describing: this idea of place and this experience of sharing things with each other, and how meaningful it is when someone shares a record with you and it comes with context. It’s a gift…

Is it too late to mow your grass? Here is the one sign your lawn is ready for winter

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

That last cut before winter is the trickiest mow of the year, and most lawn damage blamed on harsh winter weather actually starts with a badly timed final pass. Leave your grass too long and damp fall air turns it into a breeding ground for moss and snow mold, scalp it too short or mow over waterlogged turf, and the first hard freeze will weaken the roots until spring.

Because shifting fall weather rarely follows a neat schedule, watching the calendar will only steer you wrong. Instead, your lawn gives away one clear visual sign when it is ready for winter, and knowing how to spot it, alongside a few simple mower adjustments, makes all the difference before the first freeze arrives.

The surest signal it's time to pack the mower away is when your grass noticeably stops growing between cuts. Once the blades stay roughly the same height a week or two after a trim, your lawn has entered winter dormancy and no longer needs cutting.

Grass responds directly to soil and air temperatures, so most cool-season lawns continue putting on slow growth until daytime temperatures dip consistently below 50°F (and around 60°F for warm-season grasses).

As long as your turf is still actively growing, it benefits from occasional maintenance — but once temperatures drop and growth stalls, continuing to mow only stresses dormant blades that cannot repair themselves until spring.

When your grass is still putting on a little growth in late fall, a careful, well-timed trim sets it up to bounce back thicker and greener next year. Follow these four rules before storing your mower for the season:

Never scalp the lawn for its final pass of the year. Set your mower to one of its highest settings, leaving the grass around 2 to 2.5 inches tall, so the blades have enough surface area to absorb winter sunlight while shielding the roots from freezing air.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Before making your final pass, rake or blow away thick layers of fallen leaves. Wet leaves block sunlight and smother the grass underneath, and running a mower straight over a heavy blanket of them clogs your deck and leaves soggy clumps behind.

Clear stubborn, matted pine needles in seconds with the EGO Power+ 56V Cordless Blower. Blasting up to 880 CFM and 200 MPH, its lightweight carbon-fiber frame, digital status display, and brushless motor deliver gas-rivaling muscle without the fumes or hassle.

Fall rain can leave lawns saturated for days at a time. Never mow wet grass or soggy soil, as heavy mower wheels compact the ground, tear out weakened roots, and leave muddy ruts that linger until spring. Wait for a dry, mild afternoon when the turf feels firm underfoot.

Even if your lawn looks a little shaggy, keep the mower in the shed whenever frost is on the ground or a hard freeze is in the forecast. Walking on or cutting frozen grass snaps the brittle blades, leaving brown, scorched patches that take months to recover.

Right now, it's down to $1,899 (originally $2,499) after a 24% discount.

#3360. Man Found Guilty of Igniting Blaze That Became the Devastating Palisades Fire

A jury found a former Los Angeles resident guilty of starting what became the deadly Palisades Fire of January 2025, the city’s most destructive wildfire in its history.

Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, was convicted of one count of destruction of property by means of fire and one count of arson affecting property used in interstate commerce. Federal prosecutors accused Rinderknecht of intentionally starting the original blaze, known as the Lachman fire. While the initial fire was quickly suppressed, unbeknownst to firefighters and other authorities at the time, embers of it continued to burn underground. On Jan. 7, heavy winds reignited the fire, causing it to surface and spread. The ensuing Palisades fire was one of the most destructive wildfires in Los Angeles history, killing 12 people and decimating 23,448 acres of land and nearly 7,000 structures across the Pacific Palisades region.

“Twelve people lost their lives and thousands lost their homes because of Jonathan Rinderknecht’s malicious conduct,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche in a statement. “Thanks to the persistence and hard work of our prosecutors in the Central District of California, he will be held accountable.”

“Jonathan Rinderknecht deliberately ignited a fire that killed 12 people and devastated an entire community,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli. “We were determined to hold him accountable, and today’s guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended.”

After a federal jury in June deadlocked in favor of acquittal in Rinderknecht’s first trial in June, federal prosecutors narrowed their case to charge him with the two arson-related felonies rather than the three charges in the mistrial.

Steve Haney, the man’s lawyer for both trials, told the Los Angeles Times that they planned to appeal Friday’s verdict. “We are disappointed in the verdict, but respect the jury process,” Haney told the publication. “After a lengthy deliberation, they clearly gave this case a great deal of consideration.” Trending Stories Patrick Stewart Cause of Death Revealed Selena Gomez Shares Her Reaction to Martin Short Ruining Her Wedding Cake ‘Yes, Dear’ Star Anthony Clark's Cause of Death Revealed Marlon Jackson Reveals Stage 4 Prostate Cancer Diagnosis Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

The prosecution argued that Rinderknecht, who was working on New Year’s Eve as an Uber driver on Dec. 31, 2024, was angry and frustrated because he was unable to find companionship on New Year’s. According to an affidavit from an investigator for the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, two of his passengers described him as “agitated and angry” that night. He allegedly drove to a Pacific Palisades trailhead, where he repeatedly listened to and watched a music video for the rap song, “Un Zder, Un Thé,” about despair, and tried calling an old friend, but was unable to connect with them.Prosecutors said that Rinderknecht started the Lachman Fire just after midnight, and that around 12:12 a.m. on Jan. 1, 2025, environmental sensing platforms indicated the Lachman fire had begun. They said that Rinderknecht called 911 several times, but didn’t get through because his iPhone was out of range. By the time he finally connected with the police, the fire had already been reported by others in the neighborhood.

During his call with police, per the affidavit, Rinderknecht also allegedly typed a question into ChatGPT: “Are you at fault if a fire is lift [sic] because of your cigarette?” ChatGPT allegedly responded “Yes.”

#3356. Patrick Stewart Cause of Death Revealed

Patrick Stewart‘s cause of death has been revealed.

The beloved English actor died at age 86 on Oct. 28 in his Los Angeles home. His death was confirmed by a statement on his social media, which added that the cause was “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and lewy body dementia.”

His death certificate, obtained by People, lists cardiopulmonary arrest as his cause of death, and neurocognitive disorder with Lewy body as an underlying condition. TMZ was first to report the news.

The Emmy-winning performer, known for both his good natured persona and indelible roles in popular franchises like Star Trek and X-Men, was adored by his collaborators and the public alike. Stewart’s career spanned decades with work across more than five dozen films and over 50 television appearances, from X-Men and Star Trek to Dune and American Dad. Trending Stories Patrick Stewart Cause of Death Revealed Selena Gomez Shares Her Reaction to Martin Short Ruining Her Wedding Cake ‘Yes, Dear’ Star Anthony Clark's Cause of Death Revealed Marlon Jackson Reveals Stage 4 Prostate Cancer Diagnosis

His stage roles also ran the gamut from Shakespeare’s Scottish play to Waiting for Godot to his memorable one-man version of A Christmas Carol. In 1966, he joined the Royal Shakespeare Company and he remained with the storied company until 1982. During his tenure at the Royal Shakespeare Company, Stewart featured in numerous productions, including Hamlet, King Lear, and The Taming of the Shrew. He would continue appearing onstage throughout his career, notably joining longtime friend and actor Ian McKellen for Waiting for Godot in 2009 and again in 2014.

In a wave of tributes from Hollywood following his death, William Shatner remembered Stewart, who succeeded him as captain of a Star Trek franchise. “Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor,” wrote Shatner. “From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did.”

#3354. Atomically Thin Materials Significantly Shrink Qubits

MIT researchers use 2D materials for capacitors in quantum circuits in an effort to scale processors

Superconducting quantum processor and its microwave packaging.

Quantum computing is a devilishly complex technology, with many technical hurdles impacting its development. Of these challenges two critical issues stand out: miniaturization and qubit quality.

IBM has adopted the superconducting qubit road map of reaching a 1,121-qubit processor by 2023, leading to the expectation that 1,000 qubits with today’s qubit form factor is feasible. However, current approaches will require very large chips (50 millimeters on a side, or larger) at the scale of small wafers, or the use of chiplets on multichip modules. While this approach will work, the aim is to attain a better path toward scalability.

Now researchers at MIT have been able to both reduce the size of the qubits and done so in a way that reduces the interference that occurs between neighboring qubits. The MIT researchers have increased the number of superconducting qubits that can be added onto a device by a factor of 100.

“We are addressing both qubit miniaturization and quality,” said William Oliver, the director for the Center for Quantum Engineering at MIT. “Unlike conventional transistor scaling, where only the number really matters, for qubits, large numbers are not sufficient, they must also be high-performance. Sacrificing performance for qubit number is not a useful trade in quantum computing. They must go hand in hand.”

The key to this big increase in qubit density and reduction of interference comes down to the use of two-dimensional materials, in particular the 2D insulator hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The MIT researchers demonstrated that a few atomic monolayers of hBN can be stacked to form the insulator in the capacitors of a superconducting qubit.

Just like other capacitors, the capacitors in these superconducting circuits take the form of a sandwich in which an insulator material is sandwiched between two metal plates. The big difference for these capacitors is that the superconducting circuits can operate only at extremely low temperatures—less than 0.02 degrees above absolute zero (-273.15 °C).

Superconducting qubits are measured at temperatures as low as 20 millikelvin in a dilution refrigerator.Nathan Fiske/MIT

In that environment, insulating materials that are available for the job, such as PE-CVD silicon oxide or silicon nitride, have quite a few defects that are too lossy for quantum computing applications. To get around these material shortcomings, most superconducting circuits use what are called coplanar capacitors. In these capacitors, the plates are positioned laterally to one another, rather than on top of one another.

As a result, the intrinsic silicon substrate below the plates and to a smaller degree the vacuum above the plates serve as the capacitor dielectric. Intrinsic silicon is chemically pure and therefore has few defects, and the large size dilutes the electric field at the plate interfaces, all of which leads to a low-loss capacitor. The lateral size of each plate in this open-face design ends up being quite large (typically 100 by 100 micrometers) in order to achieve the required capacitance.

In an effort to move away from the large lateral configuration, the MIT researchers embarked on a search for an insulator that has very few defects and is compatible with superconducting capacitor plates.

“We chose to study hBN because it is the most widely used insulator in 2D material research due to its cleanliness and chemical inertness,” said colead author Joel Wang, a research scientist in the Engineering Quantum Systems group of the MIT Research Laboratory for Electronics.

On either side of the hBN, the MIT researchers used the 2D superconducting material, niobium diselenide. One of the trickiest aspects of fabricating the capacitors was working with the niobium diselenide, which oxidizes in seconds when exposed to air, according to Wang. This necessitates that the assembly of the capacitor occur in a glove box filled with argon gas.

While this would seemingly complicate the scaling up of the production of these capacitors, Wang doesn’t regard this as a limiting factor.

“What determines the quality factor of the capacitor are the two interfaces between the two materials,” said Wang. “Once the sandwich is made, the two interfaces are “sealed” and we don’t see any noticeable degradation over time when exposed to the atmosphere.”

This lack of degradation is because around 90 percent of the electric field is contained within the sandwich structure, so the oxidation of the outer surface of the niobium diselenide does not play a significant role anymore. This ultimately makes the capacitor footprint much smaller, and it accounts for the reduction in cross talk between the neighboring qubits.

“The main challenge for scaling up the fabrication will be the wafer-scale growth of hBN and 2D superconductors like [niobium diselenide], and how one can do wafer-scale stacking of these films,” added Wang.

Wang believes that this research has shown 2D hBN to be a good insulator candidate for superconducting qubits. He says that the groundwork the MIT team has done will serve as a road map for using other hybrid 2D materials to build superconducting circuits.

Dexter Johnson is a contributing editor at IEEE Spectrum, with a focus on nanotechnology.

#3352. Major privacy breaches reported in Muse AI – company responds [U]

This includes again accessing end-to-end encrypted messaging without permission, and sharing what may be the bank balances of another Muse user …

Siri AI was not the only AI app to launch back in September; Meta’s Muse AI app was launched the same month, with the company describing it as “your personal AI agent that gets things done across every part of life.”

Muse initially launched as an iPhone app, with Mac and iPad apps following shortly afterwards. It immediately moved to the top of the US App Store charts, overtaking ChatGPT. It quickly exceeded 5 million downloads following a major advertising push by Meta, and that number has since doubled.

Security researcher Patrick Wardle also discovered a zero-day vulnerability that could allow an attacker to hijack dictated prompts, directing them instead to their own server.

I said at the time that I would absolutely not be one of the millions of people using the app, and the wisdom of that decision has now been underlined by a fresh report.

Reuters now reports Meta employees discussing further breaches. This includes another example of accessing encrypted messages without permission.

The report says this appears to have been done by capturing push notifications. However, this was what the app claimed had happened in the earlier case, and it turned out not to be true. The AI Now Institute was able to replicate the problem of Muse accessing Signal messages without permission.

Another employee reported receiving unsolicited bank balances that they say appeared to be those of another Muse user.

Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

“I have never shared my bank account with Muse and never discussed any banking topic with Muse. I’m afraid it’s sending other’s bank info to me,” the staffer wrote in his post.

Meta told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents” and suggested that the bank balances may have been AI hallucinations rather than leaked information. Update: Meta has now told us that the balances were definitely hallucinations.

"AI Agent" = Malware. There are an expanding number of "I told it not to do that" cases.

The instructions (prompt) you give the agent are a tiny fraction of the total prompt context the agent uses, and Meta/Grok/etc. is not going to let you see that context. Agents harvesting your data (ex. see full disk access) and sending it to the mothership is just another revenue/training stream. Even if you are paying you are still the product.

Meta has taken issue with the messaging claims. It says that access to either notifications or messaging must be explicitly granted.

With Android, users have the option to grant apps notification access, which allows apps to see notifications as they’re received. This is something users need to opt in to and is not specific to Muse. With Mac, to allow Muse to work on your behalf, you not only need to click allow for accessibility and screen recording, but after that it takes you to a settings screen where you once again need to confirm and turn this on.

The company also implies that the experience of employees may relate to internal versions of Muse.

Employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.

I can only repeat my previous take on Muse: Nope.

Amazon has marked down Roku’s smart TVs and streaming devices as part of its Black Friday 2026 sale, taking up to $220 off the TVs and up to 50% off the streaming players—giving you a good opportunity to upgrade your home entertainment setup or simply get more out of the one you already own. Prices start at $20 for the Roku Streaming Stick HD, which works with older HD TVs, and go up to $429.99 for the 65-inch Roku Plus Series, which has a bigger 4K screen and a Mini-LED backlight.

At just $229.99, down from $349.99, the 55-inch Select Series Smart TV (2026) is an inexpensive way to get a 4K smart TV for a bedroom, apartment, or secondary living space. It offers a large enough screen for comfortable viewing from the couch, while Roku's familiar interface gives you easy access to major streaming services.

For a larger screen and better picture quality, the 65-inch Plus Series Smart TV is down to $429.99 from $649.99, saving you $220. Its 4K QLED display delivers richer colors than the entry-level Select Series, while Dolby Vision support helps bring out more detail in bright highlights and darker scenes when watching compatible content. The extra screen space also makes it a better fit for a main living room TV.

You don’t necessarily need a new television to enjoy Roku’s streaming platform, because the 2025 Streaming Stick HD can add it to the TV you already own, and right now, it’s $19, down from $39.99. It draws power from a compatible TV’s USB port and streams in 1080p, making it a good fit for older HD TVs, guest rooms, and even hotel TVs. Read PCMag’s review for more details.

For TVs that support 4K, the Streaming Stick Plus is a step up, offering sharper resolution and support for HDR10 and HDR10+ while keeping the same compact, USB-powered design as the HD model. It's currently $49, down from $34.99, and also supports Apple AirPlay for streaming content from an iPhone. You can read more about its features in PCMag's review.

For anyone looking to improve their TV's sound along with its streaming capabilities, the Roku Streambar SE combines both in a single device and is currently $89, down from $149.99. It supports 4K streaming with HDR10 and HDR10+ and uses two 1.9-inch full-range drivers with a bass port to deliver fuller audio than most built-in TV speakers.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

The best thing you can do is compare the prices with other retailers that have Black Friday sales. If that seems like too much work, you can just follow our Black Friday coverage (we're already doing all the searching and vetting for you). Some other tips are making sure you're not being sold an older or cheaper version and always reading reviews.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.
